World.title: France continues to fight devastating wildfires, while progress is made in Spain
World.content:
France continues to fight devastating wildfires, while progress is made in Spain

toggle caption Oscar del Pozo/AFP via Getty Images

SEVILLE, Spain — French President Emmanuel Macron called a crisis meeting Monday to coordinate efforts to fight the wildfires in southern France that have forced the evacuation of more than 250,000 people.

The emergency session came as the active fire in the Gironde region of southwest France slowed down overnight into Monday, offering a first sign of relief after the flames burned more than 100,000 acres.

The prefecture of Gironde said the situation overnight had remained stable, a welcome change after the wildfire came close to the wine region of Bordeaux over the weekend.

No new evacuations were ordered on Monday. Over 220,000 residents were evacuated in the region alone. But authorities took some precautionary steps, banning holiday camps for children, as Gironde is a popular tourist destination.

On the ground, firefighters worked tirelessly to make progress in a race against time before a forecast surge in temperatures this week could complicate efforts to put out the fires.

Sponsor Message

In a weekend social media post, Macron pledged long-term support for communities hit by the fires, saying: "We will rebuild, we will repair, and we will be present for as long as necessary."

toggle caption Julien de Rosa/AFP via Getty Images

In Spain, a fire in the region of Madrid that has burned over 60,000 acres was still active on Monday. Firefighting crews were making progress in keeping the blaze under control, but strong wind gusts were complicating those efforts.

That fire came close to another large blaze, in the region of Ávila‎, over the weekend. That fire has burned over 100,000 acres.

Authorities said on Sunday that the two large fires had been brought under control, after a difficult day on Saturday when authorities had openly said the two large fires were uncontained.

A third major fire in eastern Spain, in the region of Castellón, has affected about 75,000 people, with some of them evacuated and others asked to remain at their properties. That wildfire is still active, although it has slowed down, and authorities hope it will be under control by Tuesday.

On Monday, Aemet, Spain's national meteorology agency, forecast the fourth heat wave so far this summer, starting Wednesday. That leaves authorities with 24 hours to contain the wildfires before conditions worsen considerably. This summer is on track to be the hottest on record in Spain, according to Aemet.

toggle caption Oscar del Pozo/AFP via Getty Images

The devastating wildfires in Spain and France have forced more than 300,000 people to evacuate their homes.

Sponsor Message

More than 242,000 acres have been burned in France this year — a historic record — French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said Saturday.

Fires have burned over 300,000 acres already this year in Spain, up from an annual average of 250,000 acres over the past decade, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said on Saturday, placing the focus on the impact of climate change.

The fires also affected the Tour de France, the country's annual cycling race, which ended Sunday. The route for the race's final stage was shortened because security and police for the event were reassigned to assist with the fires, organizers said.



NPR's Chandelis Duster contributed to this report.

World.title: Kalshi attacks a Wisconsin law banning election bets as 'voter suppression'
World.content:
Kalshi attacks a Wisconsin law banning election bets as 'voter suppression'

toggle caption Scott Olson/Getty Images

Ann Jacobs is a commissioner with the Wisconsin Elections Commission, a quiet, low-profile state agency that oversees elections. Recently, though, her day was anything but quiet.

"I was sitting at my desk, and all of a sudden Twitter was showing a lot of alerts," said Jacobs, who watched a flood of posts inundate her screen from employees, lawyers and other boosters of the prediction market company Kalshi.

"My reaction was, boy howdy are they mad," Jacobs said.

Sponsor Message

The outrage took Jacobs aback because of what set off the attacks: a commission advisory informing voters that they cannot place a bet in an election in which they cast a ballot.

Wagering on such a race could disqualify a ballot, or even result in a referral to state prosecutors, according to the commission's statement.

This is not a new policy. The advisory was simply stating the basics of a Wisconsin election law originally passed in 1849, Jacobs said.

"You can't be a felon on active supervision and vote. If you're 17, you can't vote, and betting on an election where you vote, it's the same thing, it's not allowed," she said.

Jump ahead to 2026, and Kalshi, the company leading the prediction market craze, is criticizing the law, calling it "bananas," "illegal" and a type of "voter suppression."

Watching employees of the multibillion-dollar company whip up a social media frenzy against an antebellum Wisconsin law left Jacobs puzzled.

To her, pointing out election law months before an election was "simply responsible work by a government entity."

The commission was spurred to issue the warning as prediction markets have become increasingly mainstream and a more prominent part of political discussions.

"We want people voting for the person they think will do the best job at the position they are being elected to. We don't want people voting for someone who isn't the best person for the job simply because it is going to line a voter's pocket," Jacobs said.

Election expert: Betting raises election integrity concerns

Billions of dollars are traded every week on prediction market sites Kalshi and Polymarket.

Sponsor Message

Nearly half the states, including Wisconsin, are locked in legal battles with Kalshi over who should regulate prediction markets. States insist the companies are no different than gambling operators and should be subject to state gaming laws, whereas Kalshi and the Trump administration say the federal government should oversee prediction markets as a financial product known as "a swap."

As the legal fights bang on, the bets keep pouring in.

Big sporting events, like the NBA Finals and the World Cup, saw tens of billions of dollars wagered. The companies expect the midterm elections to be another massive event.

Yet that vision conflicts with another reality: Election betting is illegal in some or all circumstances in 32 states, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

"There should be absolutely no money involved in the outcome of our democracy. We should be voting on candidates for their positions and policies to represent us, not because we can make a buck," said Matt Barreto, director of the UCLA Voting Rights Project.

Election betting presents numerous possible election integrity issues, he said.

Foreign actors or partisan interests could use prediction markets to make a candidate appear more popular than they are in an effort to influence turnout.

Then there's the potential for insider trading, something that has dogged the prediction market industry, where everyone from President Trump's teleprompter operator to a special forces soldier has been accused of trading with confidential information. Kalshi has said it blocked "dozens" of political campaign staffers who have tried to bet on their own candidates since May.

Imagine, Barreto said, how this could play out during the midterms.

Say a poll worker places a bet on one candidate, and in order to make money, the person slows down the vote count or does an intentional undercount to change the real election result.

Sponsor Message

"If we found people who were somehow connected to either political campaigns or to the administration of elections, in the secretary of state's office or county elections office, were somehow involved in this, in the same way that Pete Rose tarnished the sanctity of baseball," said Barreto, referring to the baseball legend who was banned from the sport in 1989 in a betting scandal.

Charles Stewart, who runs MIT's Election Data and Science Lab, said most states have vote-counting checks that would prevent such manipulation from happening, but it is a hypothetical that could become part of already heated political discourse.

"If you are looking for a reason to be skeptical about election results, election officials trying to manipulate them for financial gain becomes another straw to grasp at," Stewart said. "However, these people don't need prediction markets to concoct some conspiracy theory to explain away why their candidate lost."

Kalshi declined to comment.

The company has argued that election betting will engage people who might not have cared otherwise about politics. The company argues that states like Wisconsin trying to prevent election betting are engaged in "voter suppression," because some voters who place wagers on a race might also be motivated to vote in the election — when they otherwise might not go to the polls.

Barreto does not buy that argument.

"If they sincerely cared about voter suppression, they would use some of their profits to set up a charity to mobilize the vote," he said.

Kalshi is not backing turn-out-the-vote efforts.

The company did recently launch something else: a midterm election dashboard to allow traders to monitor and place money on dozens of races at once.

World.title: Baltimore will turn 911 into more than just an emergency number
World.content:
Baltimore will turn 911 into more than just an emergency number

toggle caption Matt Gush/Getty Images

In March in a McDonald's parking lot off a busy Baltimore street, mental health clinician Michala Williams met a 38-year-old woman in a car.

"So, you called the police for help?" Williams asked the woman, who was sobbing uncontrollably and said she sometimes thinks about harming herself.

This story was produced in partnership with KFF Health News.

She told Williams she has children ranging from age 2 to 22, she was dealing with health issues, and that her fiancé had recently been jailed. She felt so overwhelmed she couldn't eat.

The woman, who asked not to be named so that she could freely discuss her mental health, explained she'd tried to get help the previous month by driving to the hospital but got pulled over on the way because her car registration had expired.

"I don't care if I get pulled over," she said. "But I was saying, 'I don't know what to do. I just want to go to the hospital.'"

Sponsor Message

The officer arrested her for acting erratically, so instead of going to the hospital she went to jail.

"I had to sit inside of a cold cell. I couldn't use the bathroom or anything," the woman said.

On the day she met Williams, she'd decided to call 911. The dispatcher recognized the woman didn't need a police response but instead needed one of Baltimore's mobile crisis teams, which send a clinician and a peer counselor to meet people in mental health distress.

By the end of an hourlong conversation, Williams set the woman up with referrals to a psychiatrist, a therapist, legal help and a case manager to determine if her child with autism was eligible for government services.

toggle caption Scott Maucione/WYPR

"She's been through a lot of trauma, and no one is going to deny that," Williams said. "But I now have to take all of that and decide, 'OK, here's steps 1, 2, and 3,' because we got to find a little bit of sliver of something to give her some hope that there's help out here."

Problem solving 24/7, without badges, guns or handcuffs

For years, the mobile crisis teams, which are overseen by Behavioral Health System Baltimore, a nonprofit that acts as the city's mental health department, have diverted calls from police to mental health professionals. However, the units have a limited scope, focused on people in mental health crises.

Sponsor Message

Now Baltimore is tapping into some of the roughly $400 million it has received from opioid-related legal settlements to build out a broader service to operate around the clock and respond to other kinds of crises when police aren't needed.

Baltimore logged 1.68 million calls to 911 in 2024, but tens of thousands of them didn't require traditional emergency services, like police, firefighters, or EMTs, according to Tahir Duckett, an expert in community safety at Georgetown Law.

Instead, the calls were about, for example, a homeless person who fell asleep in a store, a person who seemed confused in a public park, and someone who was yelling at passersby on the street.

Such calls "don't require a badge, a gun, and handcuffs to resolve," Duckett said.

Often those people end up in jail instead of getting the help they need, he said.

A study recently found that when a non-law enforcement team responded to 911 calls in Durham, N.C., it resulted in fewer arrests than when police responded — especially for callers who were Black, men, or ages 25-39.

Police responses can also lead to trauma for that person or a less satisfactory outcome than another community service response would produce, Duckett said.

The idea behind the Baltimore mobile crisis teams — and the new service — is to find out what people in crisis may need and how to connect them to those resources instead of arresting them.

How a legal windfall will pay for expanded 911

From 2021 to 2025, Baltimore's homicide rate decreased by 60%, setting records for the drop in violence. But at the same time, drug overdoses made national records, as about 1,000 people here died of an overdose each year from 2020 to 2023.

In 2018, Baltimore opted out of a global settlement that other jurisdictions made with opioid makers and distributors and instead sued them independently.

As these opioid-related lawsuits settled, city officials decided that the settlement awards it receives must be spent on drug-related harms — or on services that help prevent addiction such as housing support, healthcare, and education.

Sponsor Message

One new program seeks to directly address overdoses by placing boxes of the overdose reversal drug naloxone at every subway stop.

Expanding 911 services is part of a larger strategy to beef up city services, with $15 million in settlement funds allocated so far, according to Sara Whaley, Baltimore's director of overdose response.

Whaley hopes the expansion will help the city think differently about how it responds to residents in crisis — regardless of why they're calling 911.

She views the calls as an opportunity to help solve a problem rather than be punitive. "What are the wraparound services and support that can help prevent them from being involved in this, in that emergency system?" she said.

For example, the person falling asleep in a store may need connection to community housing. The goal is to reduce violence, get people proper resources, and avoid the cycle of incarcerating people dealing with poverty, addiction, and mental health.

"The right response at the right time"

Rebecca Neusteter, executive director of the Health Lab at the University of Chicago, studies the impacts of services like these. She said they offer peace of mind for callers that "they're going to be met with the right response at the right time."

"We also see responders themselves feeling like they have a better toolbox in their ability to pursue actual resolution to these calls," she said.

To expand its system, Baltimore looked to cities — including Durham — that have adopted similar models to reroute callers who don't need emergency responders.

Durham's diversion program is called the Holistic Empathetic Assistance Response Team, or HEART. The program estimates it has diverted more than 12,000 calls in four years. It said police backup was needed for only 0.02% of those calls and that response times have improved for all types of 911 calls.

Durham has collected descriptions of the HEART calls, showing that nonpolice responders in Durham have helped with everything from finding housing for a woman fleeing domestic violence to setting up medical appointments for a homeless veteran.

Sponsor Message

In one case, a hotel manager called 911 asking for help finding a blind man housing for the night, since the hotel didn't have accessible rooms available. The HEART responders booked him a room and the next day provided a ride to meet with an organization that could help secure housing.

This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with WYPR and KFF Health News.

World.title: In Memphis, an 'anti-crime' task force quietly turned into an ICE crackdown
World.content:
In Memphis, an 'anti-crime' task force quietly turned into an ICE crackdown

toggle caption George Walker IV/AP

MEMPHIS, TENN. — When President Trump announced an anti-crime task force for Memphis last fall, federal and local officials never mentioned immigration enforcement as a goal.

But the influx of federal agents into the city has led to widespread immigration arrests — a majority without criminal convictions, according to an Institute for Public Service Reporting data analysis.

NPR reviewed arrest data and spoke with lawyers, immigrants, activists and community members to piece together the task force's impact on Memphis over the past 10 months.

It found paralyzed immigrant neighborhoods, where scenes played out reminiscent of Chicago and Minneapolis at the height of targeted federal immigration enforcement actions. Aid networks ramped up their work to help immigrants too fearful to leave their homes. Hotlines rang out with calls from panicked immigrants. And routine traffic stops led to immigration arrests.

Sponsor Message

All of this has happened without the glare of the national spotlight and amid muted public outcry, as local and state leaders have largely cooperated with the federal government.

Meanwhile, Trump has said he has plans for similar task forces elsewhere, particularly in Republican-led states where he has more political buy-in.

toggle caption Brad Vest for NPR

"All roads lead to immigration enforcement with this administration," says Chioma Chukwu, executive director at American Oversight, a nonprofit, nonpartisan watchdog that has been investigating the Trump administration's use of multi-agency task forces like the ones in Memphis and Washington, D.C.

She says one of the aspects her organization is tracking is the way in which the administration has consistently conflated illegal immigration with crime, to help in what she calls "mission creep," particularly in places where anti-crime rhetoric might be more popular. .

"This administration has used crime as a pretext for furthering and advancing its immigration enforcement agenda because they understand that immigration may not be top of mind in maybe non-border states in the way that it is in border states," says Chukwu.

Trump launched the task force last fall, along with Tennessee Republican Gov. Bill Lee, despite crime being at a 25-year low in the city. For nearly a year, more than a dozen federal agencies as well as hundreds of Tennessee National Guard members have been working closely with local and state law enforcement.

Sponsor Message

Trump called it a "replica" of the ongoing anti-crime task force in Washington, D.C. saying it would focus on "dangerous career criminals." That task force also had a significant immigration enforcement aspect to it.

"President Trump's crime task forces in Washington D.C. and Memphis have yielded tremendous results for local communities," White House spokesperson Abigail Jackson wrote to NPR when asked about the immigration aspect of the task forces, listing impacts without providing evidence.

The vast majority of the arrests made by the task force — whether for immigration or otherwise — have been for nonviolent crimes, according to data from the city.

Loading...

Loading...

Emily Williams, a spokesperson for the U.S. Marshals Service, which leads the Memphis task force, reiterated that immigration enforcement is "only one aspect" of the mission and denied that anyone is being targeted.

"Our primary focus is violent offenders. We arrest anyone who is breaking the law — if you are in the country illegally, you are committing a crime," Williams wrote in a statement.

Advocates braced for arrests

When the Memphis task force was announced, immigration lawyers and advocates in the city had already been tracking what was happening in D.C. and preparing.

The immigrant community in Memphis — mostly Hispanic and Haitian — is only about 10% of the city's population, but it's also the fastest growing segment, according to U.S. Census data.

"As soon as the announcement came out, I was really clear-eyed about what was going to be happening," says Casey Bryant, executive director of Advocates for Immigrant Rights in Memphis, which provides legal services.

Bryant remembers that much of the media coverage at the time was about the deployment of hundreds of Tennessee National Guard members to the city, but that felt like a distraction. "It was really going to be about the federal agencies that were riding the coattails of the National Guard."

Sponsor Message

Maria Oceja, a co-founder of Vecindarios 901, a local rapid-response network that has been tracking U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity in the city since the first Trump administration, says she began making the rounds to local officials, asking if they thought the task force would be focused on immigration enforcement.

toggle caption Brad Vest for NPR/Brad Vest

"I was like, they're not coming to Memphis for just crime. I'm pretty sure this is going to be an ICE operation," she remembers telling them.

Oceja felt like her fears were confirmed when members of Trump's administration visited Memphis to roll out the task force in October. Stephen Miller — the chief architect for the White House immigration agenda — told the assembled law enforcement officers: "You are unleashed."

She says that very first evening, the hotline her organization runs received so many calls, they had to have four people answer it simultaneously throughout the night. That lasted for months.

'We weren't sleeping'

The first few months of the Memphis Safe Task Force brought hundreds of immigration arrests, a sixfold increase from previous months, despite local and federal officials continuing to say the task force was focusing on crime. A vast majority of those arrests were for people with no criminal convictions, according to analysis of those arrests by the Institute for Public Service Reporting in Memphis.

Those trends mirror the first months of the D.C. Safe and Beautiful Task Force.

Loading...

Loading...

The Memphis Safe Task Force does not release a breakdown of its arrests. A dashboard maintained by the city, which has gotten pushback from the community for its lack of detail and transparency, had immigration arrests listed for the first few weeks, but those numbers disappeared.

Much of the task force's operations have been focused on traffic stops, and the immigration arrests seem to have happened largely during those, according to activists and constitutional observers.

"That's been the main way that families have been separated," says Oceja, of Vecindarios 901, noting that in the first few months, law enforcement was "pulling people over left and right."

She says the hotline was getting so many calls reporting traffic stops on well-traveled routes that they eventually set up a Facebook channel where people could receive alerts on the safest ways to go.

"We weren't sleeping," she remembers. "It was a very, very traumatic time for our community."

toggle caption Brad Vest for NPR

Hunter Demster, a Memphis resident who films as much task force activity as he can, says the traffic stops seem to be centered in the two main Hispanic neighborhoods in the city.

Sponsor Message

"It was very evident that this was an immigration operation at its core," he says. "This isn't necessarily about finding the worst of the worst or fixing crime. It's about targeting Black and brown folk."

toggle caption Brad Vest for NPR

Community leaders say the shock the task force brought was immediate and far-reaching, mirroring scenes from places like Minneapolis and Chicago during the height of immigration raids, as people were afraid to leave their homes for fear of being detained.

"There was a spike of fear and panic," says Mauricio Calvo, president and CEO of Latino Memphis. "Kids were not going to school, people were not showing up to work. We were getting calls from medical providers saying people were not coming in."

He says now, 10 months into the task force presence, the number of arrests seems to have slowed and many have been trying to return to some sense of normalcy.

A lingering presence

toggle caption Brad Vest for NPR

But throughout Memphis, signs of the federal task force – which does not have a set end date — are still constant, from Tennessee National Guard troops stationed in grocery store parking lots and along tourist areas of downtown to convoys of unmarked SUVs with tinted windows lining thoroughfares.

Mutual aid groups are still seeing high demand too. Amber Hampton runs a makeshift food pantry out of her garage in a suburb of the city. She's parked her family car in the driveway to bring in shelves, filling them with canned food, dry goods, toiletries and cleaning supplies.

toggle caption Brad Vest for NPR

Hampton works with a network of volunteers to deliver boxes of groceries to immigrant families impacted by the task force, many of whom are still limiting their time out of the house to only the most essential activities.

She says when the federal immigration raids in Minneapolis were happening in January, she remembered thinking it was really similar to what was happening in Memphis, except without nearly as much attention, in part because local officials were welcoming.

toggle caption Brad Vest/for NPR

But she does think that there is a shift in perception starting to happen in the Memphis community at large, as the impact that the task force has had on the immigrant community starts to become more apparent.

Sponsor Message

"I think as more stories are coming out, people are realizing that what is happening on the ground, is not what they were sold," Hampton says.

A teen's arrest

toggle caption Brad Vest for NPR

When 18-year-old Yasser Lopez thinks back to the moment he was detained by federal immigration officers in Memphis in February, he remembers being confused, wondering what he did wrong.

"But then I remembered that this is the new norm," he says in Spanish through a translator. "This is what has been happening all around the city. Now, it just happened to me."

Lopez was arrested for being in the country illegally while riding as a passenger in a car on his way to a soccer game, according to the Department of Homeland Security. The car was stopped by Memphis police, and immigration agents followed. He was sent to a nearby detention facility and held without bond.

toggle caption Brad Vest/for NPR

His classmates staged a walkout in protest of his detention and his case was covered in the local media, then picked up by the ACLU. Lopez was later released after a U.S. district court judge found his arrest and detention violated his due process.

Ronnie Davis, a barber in the Frayser neighborhood of Memphis, was cautiously optimistic about the task force when NPR spoke with him ten months ago. But the immigration element to it — including Lopez's case, which he heard about on the news — has given him pause.

"I do not want children pulled from cars and out of schools," he says.

Davis says he does feel safer since the task force arrived, mainly because of the overwhelming presence of law enforcement now in his neighborhood, but he has noticed the impact it's had on the immigrant community, saying some of his friends have been deported.

"They are only touting the good things," Davis says about the way officials have praised the federal intervention, saying that maybe those things have benefited him. "But had I been Hispanic, I'd be terrified. If I was Haitian, I'd be terrified."

Sponsor Message

Local cooperation

One of the most notable differences between Memphis and other cities that have experienced federal interventions under this administration is the cooperation at the state level, making it hard for local pushback to take root.

In a visit to Memphis in March, Trump declared the Memphis Safe Task Force a success, saying that crime had been "fixed" in the city. He sat at a table with Gov. Lee, along with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Stephen Miller, the architect of Trump's immigration policy.

"What has happened here has created a generational change," Gov. Lee said, focusing entirely on crime reduction without mentioning immigration enforcement, but thanking Miller directly for his focus on the task force.

Crime has gone down in Memphis since the task force was launched, according to local police data. But crime in the city has fallen steadily since 2023, when it hit a near-record high.

toggle caption George Walker IV/AP

Memphis Mayor Paul Young, a Democrat, was not at that roundtable, telling local press a "personal" matter kept him from attending.

At his own press conference later, Young talked about wanting to advocate for the community as best he could with the federal resources.

When asked directly about the high immigration arrests related to the task force, Young said that he was not "supportive," but could not control it, as federal and state officials were in agreement.

"My goal is to make sure that I can control what I can control. And there's no mayor in America that can control the immigration aspects of this," he said.

World.title: Philanthropist behind Canadian human rights museum says family pausing funding over Palestinian exhibit
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Winnipeg philanthropist who played a critical role in bringing the Canadian Museum for Human Rights to the city says her family is pausing any financial support for the institution over concerns around an exhibit on the displacement of Palestinians.

Gail Asper said she found elements of the exhibit — titled Palestine Uprooted: Nakba Past and Present — compelling, from interviews with displaced Palestinians to artifacts including people's property deeds and keys for their former homes.

But she feels the way the museum describes the related history on panels in the exhibit is missing context.

The collection explores the Nakba — Arabic for "catastrophe," and the term Palestinians use to describe Israel's declaration of independence in 1948, which led to the displacement of approximately 750,000 Palestinians.

A pair of keys to a home Winnipegger Rana Abdulla's family was expelled from, in what is now Israel, is featured in the exhibit. (Tyson Koschik/CBC)

The exhibit drew criticism even before it opened at the national museum last month, including from some Jewish Canadian organizations who said there was a lack of consultation during its development, and that it fails to acknowledge the estimated 850,000 Jews who were expelled from Arab countries in the wake of Israel's creation.

In a recent interview with CBC, Asper echoed that concern and raised others about details she said were missing from the relatively small exhibit — like that Canada has listed militant group Hamas as a terrorist entity , and that Arab leaders rejected a 1947 United Nations resolution for Palestine, then under control of the British government, to be divided into Arab and Jewish states.

While the displacement of Jews in the wake of Israel's creation and the Arab rejection of the UN resolution are acknowledged elsewhere in the museum, Asper said she fears not having that context included in the Nakba exhibit could fuel antisemitism.

But her biggest concern, she said, is that "all the work that we put into this is going to be for naught, if people don't trust this museum anymore."

The exhibit "to me, brings the curatorship into disrepute," Asper said.

"If it's so small that you can't include the truth, then you need to either not do it or you need to expand it. That's a museum decision to make it so small — the museum's got lots of room. I think they have room for the truth."

A multimedia gallery on the museum's second floor that introduces visitors to a timeline of human rights acknowledges 'hundreds of thousands of people became refugees' in the 1948 Arab-Israeli war, including Palestinian Arabs and Jews from surrounding Arab countries. (Tyson Koschik/CBC)

Asper — who took over the campaign to bring the human rights museum into existence after the 2003 death of her father, philanthropist and CanWest Global Communications founder Israel Asper — said the fallout from the Nakba exhibit has felt both surreal and embarrassing.

Her family's foundation donated over $23 million toward the museum's construction, while she personally gave another $1.4 million. That's in addition to more recent contributions to the museum's fundraising efforts and exhibit development, Asper said in an email following her interview.

While the Asper Foundation stopped funding the museum's annual gala after 2023 "because of concerns about its programming," it was about to make a $50,000 donation to support a Holocaust exhibit, but has now paused that donation, she said.

Museum stands behind curation

Asper said she hopes to see an immediate review of the exhibit and the museum's policies on how it decides what to present. But she still encourages people to see the Nakba collection themselves — and look at it with a "critical eye."

And though she hopes to see changes made at the museum, in the meantime, the financial support her family would normally give will likely go toward a recent request to increase security measures at spaces like places of worship and schools in the Jewish community, she said.

"I just know that this is a disappointment for an organization that's supposed to bring people together," Asper said in her interview. "I'm always hopeful that things can be remedied, and with dialogue and understanding, we can get back on track."

A spokesperson for Marc Miller, the federal minister of Canadian identity and culture, said in an emailed statement Monday that it's "not the role of the federal government to dictate programming at Canada’s national museums." The spokesperson directed any questions about the operation of the museum and its exhibits to its chief executive officer or board of trustees.

People gathered outside the Canadian Museum for Human Rights on June 26 to protest the Nakba exhibit. (Rudi Pawlychyn/CBC)

Museum spokesperson Amanda Gaudes said the small Nakba exhibit focuses on "the impact forced displacement continues to have on the Palestinian community here in Canada, and their ongoing struggle for human rights."

In an emailed statement, Gaudes said the museum decided on that focus because Palestinian Canadian stories were underrepresented in its galleries, and "they are important to understand the landscape of human rights today."

Building an understanding of those stories and experiences "is squarely within our mandate," and focusing on them in one exhibit "does not detract or minimize experiences of Jewish people who were displaced and who have also faced human rights violations, which our galleries also share stories about," Gaudes's statement said.

The statement said telling stories of one community "in no way negates the experiences of another," and the museum stands behind its curatorial process "and our reputation as a trusted source of human rights information."

World.title: Calgary police end ground search for missing 11-year-old Parker
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. Calgary police officials give an update on the search for Parker, a missing 11-year-old boy. Calgary police say they are "refocusing" physical search efforts for 11-year old Parker, the autistic boy who went missing more than a week ago. Police search efforts will now be focused on specific information, such as tips, rather than the extensive ground searches that have been conducted since his disappearance. "Physical search efforts in his last known whereabouts and in the Nose Hill Park, including nearby waterways, have been completed," Chief Katie McLellan told reporters Monday. "However, we are not giving up." Police have carried out an extensive search to find Parker since he went missing July 16 from his day home in the 0 to 100 block of Connaught Drive N.W. Upwards of 650 people, including officers and trained volunteers, have searched day and night, with help from police dogs, bike and horse patrols, aircraft and underwater camera deployments. McLellan said police have also been in contact with rideshare and taxi companies, delivery truck businesses, truck rental agencies and railways to ensure vehicles have been searched. "Despite these exhaustive efforts, sadly, Parker has not been located," McLellan said. "The reality that Parker remains missing is difficult for all of us, especially for his family, who continues to face unimaginable uncertainty. "Parker in many ways has become one of us, and we won't stop looking to bring him home," she said. "We have a responsibility to Parker and his family to follow the evidence and make decisions based on the information available to us." An undated photo of Parker shared by the Calgary Police Service. (Calgary Police Service) Police say they've reviewed more than 600 tips and 100,000 individual CCTV clips from over 650 cameras. "As more information comes back to us, and if we have to stand up another 600 members to go and search a particular area, that's exactly what we'll be doing," McLellan said. "But for now, those specific areas where we put those hundreds of resources in, we've been through those areas multiple times now. It's about refocusing strategies." Last known whereabouts Parker was last seen July 16 at his day home between 11:08 and 11:41 a.m. The boy was then seen in the Thorncliffe neighbourhood between 12:30 and 1 p.m., acting staff Sgt. Scott Guterson said. Clothing that’s believed to belong to Parker was found at noon that same day in the 0 to 100 block of Northmount Drive N.W., police said. Police released CCTV footage of the boy they say was captured July 16 at 12:34 p.m. from a business adjacent to McKnight Boulevard and Centre Street N.W. WATCH | Police release CCTV footage of Parker taken the day he went missing: Police release new CCTV footage of missing 11-year-old Calgary boy | Duration 2:26 On the fifth day searching for Parker, police released a video of the boy recorded Thursday at a business in the area of Centre Street N.W. and McKnight Boulevard. Investigators also gave an update on the scope of the search. Police also released CCTV footage of the boy taken at 12:52 p.m. on July 16 in the 5500 block of Travis Crescent N.E. WATCH | More CCTV footage of Parker: CCTV footage of Parker, missing in Calgary | Duration 0:27 Footage released by the Calgary Police Service on July 19, shows missing 11-year-old, Parker, walking past a home on Travis Crescent N.E. on Thursday, July 16, 2026. Police have produced a map of what they believe was Parker's route the day he went missing. The map outlines his known and believed locations based on CCTV footage. Calgary police have released a map of Parker's route on July 16, the day the 11-year-old boy went missing. The map outlines his known and believed locations based on CCTV footage. (Calgary Police Service) Parker was last seen shirtless, wearing grey shorts, black Skechers shoes and black noise-cancelling headphones. He’s four feet 11 inches tall and weighs approximately 90 pounds, with brown hair and brown eyes. Police are asking anyone with information about Parker's location, or who may have CCTV or dashcam footage, to call 403-266-1234 or use the police evidence submission portal. 'We continue to ask the public for help' Guterson said the Calgary Police Service handles about 5,000 missing persons reports every year, about 250 of which are children under the age of 12. "Ninety-nine per cent of those people are found safe and well," he said. "I want to stress how deeply concerning and deeply unusual Parker's disappearance is, which is why we're going back to the public." On July 27, Guterson encouraged people to continue sharing information and searching for Parker. "It is our sincerest hope that Parker is still alive, but realistically, every day that goes by makes that hope less likely," he said. Guterson said Parker is autistic and functions at a two- or three-year-old level. He advised the public that if they come across Parker, they should not engage him, but instead call police. He said the boy is non-verbal, and gets agitated when strangers approach him. Guterson asked the public to continue checking their yards, garages, open vehicles, RVs, sheds, pools or anywhere else a child would go. He said Parker tends to lock doors behind him, meaning people searching their properties should take the time to check behind doors even if they're locked. 🚨 How to search for Parker on your property 🚨

Many people have asked what we mean when we ask residents to "check their property." In this video, Sergeant Chris Martin demonstrates how to properly search areas where Parker may seek shelter.

What might not make sense to you… pic.twitter.com/tMpqZl7rwy —CalgaryPolice Police officers have entered and searched homes in certain locations. Calgary police are encouraging anyone aware of vacant properties on Travis Street, Travis Crescent, Trelle Drive, Taylor Crescent, Travis Place and Thomas Street — all in the city's northeast — to contact police. Guterson said if Parker were in an abandoned or vacant home, police believe he would be able to survive on his own there. "It's our understanding that he would be able to use the tap to get water and he would know to use the fridge to get food, which is one of the reasons why we're asking those vacant homes or those homes where the occupants are on vacation to be checked and double checked," Guterson said. Police vehicles and horses at a search command post for Parker at Nose Hill Park on Saturday, July 25. (Chelsey Mutter/CBC) "To any volunteer searcher out there who is trying to help, I would say don't give up," Guterson said. "Don't give up hope. We're certainly not going to." Police warn of interfering with investigation, fake online posts Police ask that any Calgarians choosing to search on their own do not interfere with police operations. Police say they've also become aware of members of the public trespassing on private property, confronting others and encouraging people to investigate criminal tips on their own. "This behaviour is unacceptable and is putting community members at risk," said a CPS statement. "Everyone wants to find Parker, and we understand the emotions involved. But showing up at private homes, confronting residents or organizing your own investigations can hinder our efforts and draws police resources away from the search and investigation." CPS also said it is aware of AI-generated, altered and unverified images of Parker or his whereabouts circulating online, and cautioned the public against viewing or sharing the content. "Unverified images, videos and claims can create confusion, spread misinformation and divert investigative resources away from credible leads that may assist in locating Parker," CPS said in a social media post on July 18. Police also encouraged people to be mindful of GoFundMe campaigns claiming to be for Parker, as the family says there are no online fundraisers associated with him. Family issues statement In a statement on July 18, Parker's family said they have been living "every parent's worst nightmare" since he went missing. "Every hour that passes without knowing where he is or whether he is safe has been incredibly difficult for us," the family said in the statement, sent out by CPS on their behalf. The family implored people to continue searching their properties for Parker. "Parker experiences the world in his own way. He may not respond when his name is called, and he can become frightened when approached by people he does not know," the family said. "Parker is deeply loved, and he is missed immensely. We just want our son home." Alert for vulnerable children There was no Amber Alert following Parker's disappearance, as that alert is used for children believed to have been abducted. Police have said they are exploring every possibility, but do not have reason to believe Parker was abducted. On July 18, an emergency alert was broadcast for Parker after the provincial government made an exemption following a police request. WATCH | Why there are calls to expand Amber Alerts as police search for autistic Calgary boy: Stephanie Karas, a Calgary mother of two children with autism, told CBC News that the alert came too late. "We've gotten alerts for tornadoes that have not touched down. We've gotten alerts for less, so I don't know why there wasn't [one]," Karas said. Karas added that she's lobbying the municipal and provincial governments to create an emergency alert protocol specifically for situations like this. On Premier Danielle Smith's biweekly radio show on Saturday, she confirmed the province would work to make that happen. "I think it's very key to have local law enforcement have the latitude to make that call," Smith said. "We have to give law enforcement this additional tool in the event that they need it, and we'll have to make the changes to make that happen in the fall."

World.title: Toronto mayor files urgent motion demanding province 'return our waterfront' after feds reject airport plans
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Toronto's mayor filed urgent motion Monday to demand the province give back waterfront land after the federal government rejected a proposal for a jet expansion at Billy Bishop Airport.

In a post on social media platform X, Mayor Olivia Chow said she wants Little Norway Park and the Toronto Islands back in the control of the municipality.

"Council has formally opposed the unacceptable overreach. We still do," she said. "Return our waterfront to us."

CBC Toronto has reached out to the Transportation Ministry for comment.

Chow’s motion, seconded by Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik, comes after federal Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon announced Friday the government would be "exclusively" focused on approved safety upgrades already underway at Billy Bishop, rather than on building the airport out to allow jets to land.

The conclusion was based on public consultations that garnered more than 87,000 responses with nearly 87 per cent of respondents opposed to changes, a spokesperson for MacKinnon said. But the minister left the door open for a potential change of course in future years, framing the decision as "at this stage," instead of a final one.

Ford's proposal to extend the airport's runway 600 metres west — on top of the 150-metre runway end safety zones already in the offing — drew criticism from environmental and community advocates over concerns around the project's effect on noise, traffic and pollution levels, as well as affordable housing and the Toronto waterfront itself. (Patrick Morrell/CBC News)

Ontario Premier Doug Ford's proposal to extend the airport's runway 600 metres west — on top of the 150-metre runway end safety zones already in the offing — drew concern from environmental and community advocates over noise, traffic and pollution levels, as well as affordable housing and the Toronto waterfront itself.

More than 6,000 lawn signs were distributed across Toronto by advocacy groups NoJetsTO and Environmental Defence, with thousands of residents sending letters to their local Member of Parliament. On Sunday, the two groups hosted a celebration to commemorate the power of community.

Liberal MP Chi Nguyen (Spadina—Harbourfront) told CBC Radio's Metro Morning her office heard from nearly 7500 residents, with almost 3,000 of them partaking in the public consultation process.

"We are all thinking about what happens in Ontario and Toronto in terms of being ready and resilient in terms of our economy, but we have to do this [by] thinking about what's right for Toronto," she added. "Toronto's waterfront has to grow with our community and not at its expense."

Province will continue 'to work to advance the expansion'

Ontario Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria said in a post on X Friday night that the provincial government still has plans for the airport and looks forward to "continuing to work to advance the expansion."

He said the plan would ensure the project addresses potential noise and environmental impacts, expands Little Norway Park, protects public spaces and supports new housing opportunities in the area.

On Saturday, Ford’s office sent CBC Toronto a statement that replicated Sarkaria's statement verbatim. Asked for comment on Chow's motion Monday, Ford's office directed CBC Toronto to its Saturday statement.

On Sunday, advocacy groups NoJetsTO and Environmental Defence hosted a celebration to commemorate the power of community. (Mercedes Gaztambide/CBC)

Sarkaria is set to host a news conference in St. Thomas, Ont., Tuesday morning.

John Gradek, a faculty lecturer in aviation management and supply networks at McGill University, said he wasn’t surprised by the federal government’s decision.

"We've had enough opposition in the marketplace, whether it's local citizens or whether it's local MP's and the media," he told CBC Radio’s Metro Morning Monday. "There really wasn't any data that was really available to us."

In her post to social media, Chow said the city has been demanding to see the plans for the airport, but the Toronto Port Authority has actively tried to hide them. She added the city has researched the impacts on housing, congestion and the environment and found the project would most benefit Wall Street bankers at JP Morgan.

According to Gradek, Toronto’s Pearson International Airport is more than satisfactory for the city.

"There is no [dire] need to create more capacity," he said, noting Billy Bishop plays a more niche role in serving the local market.

Despite this, the need might grow in the next generation, which may be why the federal government didn’t entirely close the door on the opportunity, Gradek said.

"But extending the runway by 2,000 meters and going into it and putting landfill into the lake is not the answer."

World.title: Edmonton mops up — again — in its rainiest summer on record
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Edmonton's soggy summer has officially set a new seasonal record.

The news from Environment Canada comes as the city mops up from a Saturday evening storm that rolled through the capital city region, dropping 30 millimetres of rain from 9 p.m. to 10 p.m. Wind speeds averaged 39 km/h during that time, while a maximum speed of 94 km/h was recorded by Environment Canada, said meteorologist Jennifer Kowal.

After the weekend storm, Edmonton has seen 503.7 millimetres of rain this summer, Kowal told CBC News on Monday. The previous rainfall record was 417.1 millimetres in 1953.

“It really looks like the increased temperature this summer and the water on the ground is going to just continue this pattern, at least for the foreseeable future,” said Kowal.

The Saturday storm came after multiple severe thunderstorm warnings and watches were issued by Environment Canada for much of central Alberta, including Edmonton.

On Monday, the city issued a statement detailing the impact of the powerful storm, which closed roads, flooded neighbourhoods, shut down outdoor events and downed trees.

LISTEN | Why is it raining so much?: Edmonton AM 8:42 What is driving this summer’s severe weather? The most recent major storm in Edmonton happened on Saturday, bringing floods, sewer backups, power outages, and fallen trees and branches throughout the city. Environment Canada says about 30 millimetres of rain fell during the storm, which brought winds of up to 84 kilometres per hour. Kyle Brittain is an Alberta-based weather specialist.

Post Malone concert cancelled

One of the Saturday night’s biggest incidents took place at Commonwealth Stadium, where American rapper Post Malone was playing his second of two back-to-back concerts at the outdoor venue.

Saturday's rainfall damaged parts of the stadium and sent about 31,000 fans scurrying for cover.

Stadium staff used audio messaging and the venue’s jumbotron to ask attendees to move to the open-air buildings into sheltered areas, such as the stadium’s concourse which the city said is large enough to hold the fans.

“The safety of fans, staff, crew and artists is of utmost importance,” the city said in its release.

All of Commonwealth Stadium’s emergency protocols were followed, and no injuries were reported, according to the city.

The concert was ultimately cancelled and refunds have been issued to ticket holders by Ticketmaster and Live Nation, the release said.

WATCH | Concertgoers reflect on Edmonton storm: Sudden storm wallops Edmonton, soaks concertgoers | Duration 2:07 Thousands of people were forced to quickly leave a Post Malone concert at Edmonton’s Commonwealth Stadium because of a sudden, heavy rainstorm. The city was hit was more than 30 millimetres of rain in an hour, knocking out power and flooding some areas.

Some roads, facilities remain closed

Crews were still working Monday to reopen roadways, clear debris and assess damage, but City of Edmonton infrastructure has largely withstood the heavy rainfall this summer, the city said in its news release.

Fallen trees and flooding closed multiple roadways in Edmonton on Saturday and into Sunday, including Yellowhead Trail, Whitemud Drive, Groat Road and Connors Road. These roads are now open, the city said.

The 130th Avenue and 107th Street intersection remains closed, while 178th Street’s ramp to Whitemud Drive has been reduced to one lane until repairs are complete, according to the city.

Many city recreation facilities and attractions are closed due to the storm, including:

Peter Hemingway Aquatic Centre at Coronation Park Sports and Recreation Centre

The main pool, hot tub and sauna at Grand Trunk Fitness and Leisure Centre

The Indigenous Peoples Experience at Fort Edmonton Park.

The city said it’s monitoring trail conditions in the river valley, and asked residents to exercise caution in the area.

“The North Saskatchewan River is powerful and unpredictable. Higher water levels, swift currents, submerged debris and unstable riverbanks can create dangerous conditions,” the release said, adding that if water rises to unsafe levels, the city will post closure signs and provide updated trail conditions online.

WATCH | Edmontonians clean up after summer storm: Severe thunderstorm soaks Edmonton, cancels concert | Duration 2:04 A Post Malone concert in Edmonton was cut short Saturday night, when a severe thunderstorm swept into the city. As CBC’s Sam Brooks reports, Edmontonians are once again cleaning up debris and pumping out flood water after another summer storm.

Administration asking province for funds

The city said June’s storms have prompted it to apply for the province’s Hazard Assistance and Resilience Program (HARP), which asks Alberta to reimburse municipalities for up to 90 per cent of eligible disaster costs.

June’s storms caused roughly $26 million in uninsurable loss and damage, the city said. According to the Insurance Bureau of Canada, as of mid-July, Edmonton storms have caused $230M in insured damages since May .

“The city continues to assess the impacts from July storms and will submit further HARP applications by the end of August,” it said. “Where possible, the city has leveraged existing warranties and insurance.”

World.title: Police believe at least 3 suspects involved in deadly Seattle festival shooting
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Police now say there were at least three suspects involved in a food festival shooting near Seattle's Space Needle over the weekend, and one of them was among those killed in the violence.

In a document filed in juvenile court in Seattle, where a 15-year-old arrested in the case was making an initial appearance Monday, police said they believe there were at least three shooters: the 15-year-old; an acquaintance who died at the scene; and "at least one other unknown suspect."

"Based on the evidence at the scene, investigators believe" the 15-year-old "and one of the deceased engaged in a gunfight with at least one other unknown suspect," the document said.

The teen was being held in juvenile detention for investigation of firearms violations and first-degree assault ahead of the afternoon court appearance, Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson said at a news conference.

Authorities said earlier Monday they are still looking for a second suspect, but could not rule out whether that individual was among those killed.

"We are trying to identify who that person is," said Seattle police Chief Shon Barnes.

A worker cleans blood off the pavement Monday, the day after a shooting at Seattle Center. (Lindsey Wasson/The Associated Press)

Investigators had said they believed the two suspects were shooting at each other. Police said late Sunday night it was not clear whether any of the victims had been involved in the confrontation between the two shooters.

Two people died at the scene and a third died in the hospital. They were described as two men, ages 19 and 44, and a 56-year-old woman.

The four wounded included a two-year-old boy, who was in satisfactory condition Monday. The others — two men, ages 23 and 27, and a woman, 39, were discharged, a hospital spokesperson said.

Vendors were allowed to return to the sprawling campus Monday morning to clean up and collect their equipment and merchandise. Skewered squid on grills, roasted ducks in ovens and plates full of food were among the items left behind as people fled the gunfire.

Near the spot of the shooting, a stain of what appeared to be blood was still visible in the morning. A candlelight vigil was planned Monday night at the centre's International Fountain.

Tyrone Davis, assistant chief of special operations for the Seattle Police Department, speaks to the members of the media Sunday, after officers responded to a deadly shooting at a food festival that evening. (Jason Redmond/Reuters)

Guests 'took off running'

The gunfire erupted around 6 p.m. local time on Sunday in the waning hours of Bite of Seattle, an annual three-day festival that draws hundreds of food and retail vendors to Seattle Center, a sprawling park and event space in the shadow of the Space Needle. Many attendees rushed into campus buildings or ran from the park at the sound of the shots.

Dozens of officers were providing security at the event and some saw one of the suspects firing, authorities said.

A large number of police and emergency crews responded and began evacuating the area. Police then searched an IMAX theater on the grounds where they initially believed a second shooter had fled.

Adam Lombardo, who had a Burmese food stand at the festival with his spouse, described the panic of fleeing people as a "stampede." As he gathered his equipment Monday, he described how police escorted them into the crime scene to turn off their ovens and stoves.

"It's really sad because you think that three innocent people aren't getting up with their families," he said. "They just came to enjoy a food festival with people, with friends, with new friends, and they lost their lives in just what sounds like meaningless bloodshed."

A police officer stands at a closed off area Sunday. (Lindsey Wasson/The Associated Press)

Festival attendee Faith Adia Hunter said she and her friends had just gotten food from a crepe vendor when gunfire broke out out nearby. In the scramble to find safety, she and others ran into the nearby Seattle Children's Museum.

"We were about to start eating, then heard someone yell something, then we saw people start to run," Hunter said. "So we took off running, too."

Roberto Ramirez, a vendor at the event, said he heard what sounded like firecrackers before people began yelling "shooter" and frantically running.

"Suddenly everything was empty," he said. "People were freaked out."

After the initial panic, new guests continued to arrive unaware of what had happened. Police told them to leave, Ramirez said.

Estan Wakonabo said he and his girlfriend were waiting in line for a photo booth when he was shoved from behind and turned to see a rush of people fleeing.

An unidentified man is led into the scene by police after they responded to the shooting Sunday. (Lindsey Wasson/The Associated Press)

"People were hiding, were pushing, people were falling on the ground, baby strollers were falling," Wakonabo said, adding that was when he heard gunshots.

"Once I heard a 'pop, pop, pop,' that's when I knew it was a shooter," he said.

After he escorted his girlfriend to safety, Wakonabo said he returned to the scene to take photos and saw multiple victims on the ground.

The festival started in 1982 and draws 350,000 attendees, according to its website.

World.title: Upstate New York town memorializes Montreal girl allegedly killed by father
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A year after a nine-year-old girl from Montreal was found dead near a swamp in Upstate New York, local resident Bridgette Cruz says new road signs are keeping her memory alive.

The reflective signs with yellow lettering are dedicated to "Friends of Melina Frattolin." They are posted along a short stretch of Route 74 in the small lake town of Ticonderoga, N.Y. The road connects to the I-87 highway and is used by residents to get in and out of town.

Cruz, who has lived in Ticonderoga her whole life, says she was behind the initiative to post the signs after Melina Frattolin's body was found in July 2025.

Though the girl was not known to the town of about 5,000 people, Cruz said the close-knit community was rocked by the killing.

"We're separated by a border, but she's a child. It doesn't matter," she said in an interview.

"It was just gut-wrenching," Cruz added. "It really was a tragic thing that struck a lot of people….It was really hard for a lot of people to process the emotions."

Bridgette Cruz, who lives in Ticonderoga, N.Y., says new road signs are keeping the girl's memory alive. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

The girl's father, Luciano Frattolin, is on trial in the nearby hamlet of Elizabethtown, N.Y. He is charged with second-degree murder and concealment of a corpse in the death of his nine-year-old daughter.

He pleaded not guilty to both charges and maintained that his daughter had been kidnapped while the two were on their way back to Montreal after a weeklong vacation.

Cruz, a mother of three, said she vividly remembers when authorities sent out an Amber Alert for the missing girl — the panic she felt for the child and the heartbreak when her body was found. She helped organize a vigil for the Montreal girl in the following days.

But Cruz said the death continued to haunt her and she wanted a memorial that would last. She then reached out to the Department of Transportation, which runs a program for citizens to adopt a highway.

Candles are left at the side of the road for nine-year old Melina Frattollin, next to Eagle lake, near Ticonderoga, N.Y. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

Scott Cooke, a spokesperson for the department, said the program is open to anyone and can be used for memorials.

Through the program, the department erects a highway sign acknowledging the "adopters," who commit to cleaning litter off the road a few times a year for two years. The contract can then be renewed.

The signs for Melina went up in November, and Cruz said she plans to keep them in place as long as possible. The three-kilometre stretch she selected runs by the marsh where the girl was found drowned, with one sign on each end.

"I want it to be a nice resting place for her," said Cruz. "I don't want it to be a sombre place, because it is a beautiful area."

When Cruz did her first cleaning in the spring, several troopers who had participated in the search for Melina joined her, she said.

Melina Frattolin's body was found in the shallow part of a pond in the woods of Ticonderoga in a rural area of New York on July 20, 2025. (Submitted by the New York State Police)

Heath Towne sits on the Ticonderoga town board. He said murder is exceedingly rare in the area.

He added that he wasn't surprised a citizen chose to put up a sign in memorial as it's common for people to place signs and crosses by the road to honour loved ones.

"It was a very emotional thing. Any time you have something involving a child, it will stir up a lot of emotion. It's that human instinct to protect children," he said.

He expects the trial, which is expected to conclude in August, to rekindle those emotions.

World.title: Emily Wilson's translation of The Odyssey helped inspire the film. She just panned it in a new review
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

British American classicist Emily Wilson's translation of Homer's The Odyssey made waves when it was released in 2017, marking the first time a woman translated the ancient Greek epic to English.

It also served as a inspiration for British American director Christopher Nolan. In early publicity for his recently released The Odyssey, Nolan cited Wilson's controversial opening line — "Tell me about a complicated man" — as a reference point for main character Odysseus.

But Wilson's feelings about Nolan's take, which has so far made more than $600 million US since its release just over a week ago, appear more mixed, according to a new essay published online Monday in the London Review of Books (notably titled "An Uncomplicated Man").

"I was humbled to learn that Nolan has read at least the first line of my translation," she wrote. "But I would be ashamed to have written any part of this script."

WATCH | The Odyssey trailer:

Nolan film lacks depth, narrative: Wilson

The essay took issue with nearly every aspect of The Odyssey aside from its entertainment value, which is credited to the source material — "impossible to mess up entirely," wrote Wilson, who is also a classical studies professor at the University of Pennsylvania.

But the film's narrative and emotional depth is at about the same level as "an elaborate Fourth of July fireworks display," she wrote.

The movie doesn't have a through line pulling together the multitude of ideas it presents, she argued, nor does she believe it develops its characters enough to deliver a clear message.

WATCH | Wilson previously spoke with The Sunday Magazine: What surprises translator Emily Wilson about Nolan’s The Odyssey | Duration 2:10 Emily Wilson, who translated The Odyssey into English, breaks down Christopher Nolan's blockbuster version that has everyone talking about Homer this summer. Wilson spoke with Megan Williams, guest host of CBC Radio's The Sunday Magazine. CORRECTION (July 27, 2026): A previous title of this video suggested the word "slave" was not used in Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey. In fact, the term is referenced in the film.

"Nolan's Odyssey lacks many of the elements that make the poem great," the essay reads. The main couple, Odysseus and Penelope (Matt Damon and Anne Hathaway, respectively), have neither chemistry nor a deep connection, she wrote, while Tom Holland does well playing their son, Telemachus, as a man aged "20 going on 12."

Of the leading performers, meanwhile, Damon's Odysseus is "lummoxy," "neither a master storyteller nor a flirt," while Hathaway's Penelope "looks beautiful and mysterious" but is given little to do but yearn for Odysseus "for reasons unknown."

Chief among her objections was that she didn't feel the film had a clear message. When Odysseus defies the gods, for example, the act is portrayed as noble and brave, but when his second-in-command Eurylochus does the same, it is "stupid and greedy," she wrote.

On a larger scale, the Trojan War, which Odysseus helps start, is portrayed as being horrifying, with innocent civilians subjected to violence and terror. But at the same time, the final scene, where Odysseus massacres Penelope's suitors, is presented as a series of "action-movie sequences in which the reluctant warrior finally gets his hands on his bow and the blood starts flowing."

She also challenged Nolan's decision to film part of the movie in the Moroccan-occupied territory of Western Sahara, which she said "[normalized] the ongoing violence against the indigenous Sahrawi people."

Wokeness allegations

Both Nolan's and Wilson's takes on The Odyssey have received similar criticism from some right-wing users , who charge them with diverting from the source material for political means. Wilson, in particular, has received so much backlash that she has included a separate contact form on her website for "misogynistic trolling."

The war against her translation focused on her "complicated man" opening line. "Complicated" was her interpretation of the ancient Greek word polytropos, an unusual term that has in other versions been translated to "skilled in all ways," or "man of twists and turns."

For her part, Wilson defended the choice on her Substack , saying that other phrases didn't fit her meter- and pacing-related constraints, nor did she feel they were as evocative. But online critics fought back, calling it " vandalism ," "condescending" and even an " assault on a foundation of Western culture " with a " clear feminist woke agenda ."

From left, Charlize Theron, Samantha Morton, John Leguizamo, Tom Holland, Matt Damon, Anne Hathaway, Lupita Nyong'o and Zendaya attend the premiere of The Odyssey on July 14 in New York City. (Mike Coppola/Getty Images for Universal Pictures)

The Odyssey the film also garnered its own share of racist and transphobic backlash even before its release, due to its casting of Lupita Nyong'o, who is of Kenyan descent, as Helen of Troy, and Elliot Page, who is trans.

In her review, Wilson didn't take issue with the race-neutral casting itself but said there was "nothing progressive about" it, noting that most of the non-white actors' roles resembled the "Black best friend," referring to the trope of Black characters being reduced to supporting roles for (often) white leads, with no lives of their own.

Even still, she concluded that the film's release was "an event to celebrate," bringing audiences back to theatres and potentially sparking new interest in ancient Greek and the humanities.

She acknowledged that it helped propel sales of her own book and that Nolan was doing his best to "get the general public reading again." Besides, her teenagers had a good time.

World.title: Gordie Howe’s family are the 1st to cross Canada-U.S. bridge
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Gordie Howe bridge officially opened to commercial trucks and personal vehicles on Monday. The bridge between Windsor, Ont., and Detroit is named after the legendary hockey player, and officials invited Howe's family to take the first passenger car across it.

Gordie Howe's family were in the first passenger vehicle to go across the new international border span on Monday, says the Windsor Detroit Bridge Authority (WDBA).

Howe's grandson, also named Gordie, was in the Dodge Charger that made its way across.

"It just feels surreal to be the people who were chosen to do that," he told reporters.

"We got a call yesterday about that ... it just makes me think about all of the people who have worked on this bridge and all the people we've talked to today, just how happy everyone must be that this the bridge is come to fruition. It's just, it's an honour to have been the first to cross. "

Gordie Howe family members were the first to cross the Gordie Howe International Bridge Monday morning, July 27, 2026. (Susan Goodspeed/CBC)

Howe said it's been strange to observe all of the politics around the structure from afar.

"I know it's been frustrating for a lot of people. And so I think that makes today all the more amazing that it has actually opened today and a lot of people are very happy."

U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said in a Monday statement America welcomes the opening.

“Adding new capacity to one of the busiest and most economically significant border crossings between the United States and Canada,” he said.

“President Trump made the opening possible and has consistently prioritized a safer, more secure, and more prosperous North America.”

Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer drove across the bridge in a Ford Mustang, built in Michigan, to mark the opening.

"I fought to open this bridge to strengthen the economy and connect Michiganders to opportunities on both sides of the Detroit River," she said in a social media statement.

The first truck to cross the Gordie Howe International Bridge on July 27, 2026 was from Onfreight Logistics from Tecumseh, Ont. (Susan Goodspeed/CBC)

Tecumseh trucking company Onfreight Logistics is poised to be the first commercial vehicle to cross.

Bridge officials say the standard passenger vehicle toll will be $8 ($5.75 US) to cross and $12 ($8.75) per axle for commercial trucks, oversized vehicles and larger passenger vehicles.

The span provides a highway-to-highway connection between Ontario’s Highway 401 and Michigan’s Interstate-75 — with six traffic lanes, 16 toll lanes and 60 Canada and U.S. inspection lanes.

An aerial view of the Gordie Howe International Bridge the day before it opened to traffic in 2026. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

Walkers and bike riders will be allowed to go over the Detroit River on the span starting Aug. 5.

The one-lane path will accommodate two-way pedestrian traffic. The path is 2.5 kilometres long and 3.6 metres wide and connects into existing local trail networks on either side of the border.

Heavy traffic anticipated

U.S. Customs and Border Protection is reminding travellers planning trips across the bridge to be prepared and to anticipate heavy traffic.

“Being prepared will help minimize delays at the port of entry,” the CBP said in a statement.

They say to have applicable travel documents readily available, and for crossers to accurately declare all goods, alcohol, and agriculture items. And that while legal in some states, marijuana remains illegal under U.S. federal law.

Customs booths at the Gordie Howe International Bridge the day before it was set to open to passenger and commercial vehicles, July 26, 2026. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

Border mayors chime in on The Current

Windsor Mayor Drew Dilkens says he’s weighing the long-term benefits of the span versus current tensions on either side of the Detroit River.

“I just look at this and say it's taken us 25 years to build this bridge, and it will stand for more than a hundred,” he told CBC Radio's The Current.

"The disruptions that we're feeling today, it's easy to get wrapped up in the ... tweet of the day. Let's play the long game here and recognize that what we've created together will stand to the benefit of families on both sides of the border, businesses on both sides of the borders for many generations to come.”

The Current 19:23 Will the Gordie Howe bridge deliver on its promise? A multi-billion dollar bridge between Canada and the U.S. was supposed to strengthen North American supply chains and ease bottlenecks on the nearby Ambassador Bridge and Detroit-Windsor tunnel. We hear from mayors on both sides of the Detroit River about whether tariffs are putting that investment at risk.

Bryan Barnett is the Mayor of Rochester Hills, Mich., in the Detroit metro area. He also spoke with CBC Radio's The Current.

He doesn’t think the political and economic climate overshadows Monday’s opening of the bridge to traffic.

“I don't think it diminishes it because I think people understand, as Mayor Dilkens said, the long game here is what's important, and I think that's true in the trade discussions as well. I mean, Michigan is so dependent on trade with Ontario and particularly trade with Canada as well, that it just, it's too important.”

A bridge service vehicle crosses the Gordie Howe bridge July 26, 2026. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

Barnett says he’s not a fan of tariffs and doesn’t think they’ve worked well in curbing economic behaviour.

“I hope that we use the next few weeks, both the president and the prime minister and the leaders on both sides to negotiate quickly to something that doesn't end up looking like it has in the past.”

According to Dilkens, the Gordie Howe span is not a bridge over "troubled waters."

“There is no light of day between Bryan Barnett and Drew Dilkens and between most people in the United States and Canada at this point," he said.

"We are good friends, we love our friends in the United States and I don't want to let Donald Trump overshadow what is a momentous day for us here."

As unit commander in the largest homicide squad in the country, Hank Idsinga has seen more than most people would want. He discusses with Brian Lilley what it’s really like in blue, the many things that are done right and the many things done wrong, including the recent expose of corruption by some Toronto officers. The author of the new book, “The High Road: Confessions of a Homicide Cop,” Idsinga reveals the vitriolic antisemitism he saw on the force, and discusses the “abysmal” handling of anti-Israel demonstrators in Toronto.
