World.title: Twice named and shamed builder accused of leaving customers out of pocket
World.content:
A thrice-bankrupt man convicted of multiple breaches of building regulations and subject to warnings in two states is now accused of leaving customers in the lurch in a fresh jurisdiction.

An ABC investigation has found that Steve Preston, who has been named and shamed by consumer authorities in Western Australia and Queensland, is offering to build tiny homes and cabins in northern New South Wales.

Mr Preston, who has used multiple aliases over the years, presented as a "very genuine" older guy with a "solid handshake", recalled Leigh Peters, who paid $78,000 to the self-proclaimed builder to construct two tiny homes.

Do you know more about this or have a similar story? Email turner-cohen.alex@abc.net.au

WA and Queensland authorities have issued warnings about Steve Preston. (Supplied: Chris Blewitt)

Mr Peters, a father-of-two who owns a motel in Grafton, was hoping to use the self-contained units to accommodate staff amid a housing shortage in the area.

But when things started to go wrong, Mr Peters, 36, looked more deeply into the past of his builder and was shocked.

"You don't feel like when you hire a local builder in a country town, you're going to come across [someone] with a very bad history," Mr Peters said.

When contacted by the ABC, Mr Preston declined to comment, citing pending legal matters but would not say anything further about them.

Leigh Peters says he is $30,000 out of pocket over his ordeal with Steve Preston. (Supplied: Leigh Peters)

History of unlicensed work across Australia

In 2007 the Western Australia Supreme Court permanently restrained Mr Preston from representing himself as a registered builder in that state.

A press release from the consumer watchdog at the time said the court order came after he took deposits of up to $50,000 from unknowing customers in Perth, and carried out unregistered building work.

The Western Australian building regulator labelled Mr Preston a "maverick" and a "menace".

"This is about as bad as conduct that infringes the Fair Trading Act gets," then Consumer Protection Commissioner Patrick Walker said at the time in a media release.

"Mr Preston has had absolutely no regard for the law or the interests of consumers."

The back of the motel where Leigh Peters was planning to put the two cabins he had purchased. (Supplied: Leigh Peters)

In 2009, the Perth Magistrates Court and then the Midlands Magistrates Court fined Mr Preston a total of more than $60,000 for 19 charges relating to unregistered building work and excessive deposit taking.

By then Mr Preston was living in northern NSW where he had already come to the attention of the state's consumer watchdog.

NSW Fair Trading became aware of a building company that was registered to someone linked to Mr Preston.

The building company, which operated in the Tweed Shire and New England regions, had its licence cancelled because of its close associations with Mr Preston.

Mr Preston was hit with nine penalty notices by NSW Fair Trading with fines totalling $22,000 for breaches relating to failing to obtain building insurance, and for entering into building contracts without meeting proper requirements.

A customer was concerned about the quality of a shed Steve Preston built. (Supplied: Chris Blewitt)

The ABC has spoken to several people who say they have been left out of pocket. (Supplied: Chris Blewitt)

Next stop, Queensland

Mr Preston then went to Queensland, where in 2014, the Queensland Building and Construction Commission (QBCC) issued a public warning saying that Mr Preston had been conducting unlicensed building work in the Proserpine area.

"The QBCC warns all persons dealing with Steve Preston to exercise extreme caution and seek legal advice before entering into contracts or making any payments, to protect their interests," read a media release at the time.

Banned for peddling unlicensed financial advice

Before Mr Preston's foray into the world of building, the financial regulator ASIC banned him from giving financial advice due to his involvement in an unlicenced superannuation scheme.

In 2005, a Federal Court judge granting injunctions in civil proceedings brought by ASIC said Mr Preston "embarked upon a scheme which he hoped would yield him a substantial profit" which involved the "gullibility" of clients "rolling over" their superannuation into a trust account established by his company.

At least 30 people gave more than $77,000 in total to the company.

In the case of one client, the judge said it seemed their money was "then used for the company's, or Mr Preston's, own purposes", labelling it "unconscionable conduct".

Mr Preston was prevented from giving out unlicensed financial advice again.

Bankruptcy documents and warnings from regulators show he has used the aliases Steve Brown and Steve Fowler.

He was formerly known as Gordon Fowler, a name under which he declared himself bankrupt three times in 1994, 1999 and 2006.

Preston offers to supply cabins in NSW

In 2024, Mr Peters met Mr Preston, who was running a company called Clarence Product and Building Materials Supply.

Mr Peters was shown several tiny homes at a site in Grafton before he agreed to pay $80,000 for two of them to be built offsite and transported to an empty spot behind his motel business.

"It was very appealing, the price," Mr Peters said.

"And [he said] that we wouldn't need to go through council."

Leigh Peters has had no luck getting his money back, despite engaging the NSW Sheriff's Office. (Supplied: Leigh Peters)

In a statement to the ABC, Clarence Valley Council said it required development approvals for all secondary dwellings, including tiny homes.

"Some developments, such as small sheds, can be exempt from development approval," a spokesperson said.

Mr Peters said he insisted a contract be drawn up for the two tiny homes. He said, in hindsight, it was "unprofessional" that the builder had not suggested it.

The father said he received "random" text messages from Mr Preston asking for another $10,000 here, another $10,000 there, and before he knew it, he had paid the sum total of the project.

But when he visited Mr Preston's site to see the progress of his investment, he said he found "panelling slapping in the wind", shoddy tiling and a bad plaster job.

Mr Peters said the two men came to the agreement that a refund would be paid, but after a small portion was returned, the payments stopped coming.

Mr Peters took the company to the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal in April last year and won a $66,000 order for his refund.

However, Mr Peters said the payments stopped coming at the end of last year and he was still out of pocket about $30,000.

He said he chased up Mr Preston to no avail, and paid $107 to the NSW Sheriff's Office in Grafton, which "unsuccessfully" tried to enforce the court order in May.

Leigh Peters has not received a payment from Steve Preston since November last year. (Supplied: Leigh Peters)

In a statement to the ABC, a Department of Communities and Justice spokesperson said the sheriff "made multiple attempts to establish contact with the debtor", which included phone calls, letters and visiting his address.

The spokesperson said the matter "remains active".

Supplier left in lurch

Another Grafton business owner, Mick Earea of Western Pacific Steel, said Mr Preston's company Clarence Product and Materials Supply opened an account to buy steel at the beginning of last year.

Debt soon racked up, according to Mr Earea.

"I approached him [and he said] it was all going to be fixed up," he said.

Mr Earea said Mr Preston paid some of what he owed, but that he still had an outstanding debt of $7,000 for which he had received no payments since the beginning of the year.

'Needs to be stopped'

Chris Blewitt, from the NSW south coast, said he paid $63,000 to Mr Preston in 2021 but the builder failed to complete two sheds and decking in his backyard.

The 49-year-old said the job was supposed to be done in six weeks.

Steve Preston builds a shed in Chris Blewitt's backyard. (Supplied: Chris Blewitt)

He said the offer was appealing, especially as the area, near Batemans Bay, was recovering from devastating bushfires at the time and builders were in short supply.

"The way he talked made you feel like he was your mate and he was helping you build something in your backyard rather than a business," Mr Blewitt said.

He said the only thing he had as a contract was a handwritten quote on a piece of paper.

Mr Preston asked for an initial $15,000 to buy building materials, which the Blewitt family transferred.

Work was being carried out in his backyard, so when Mr Preston asked for more money, Mr Blewitt saw nothing wrong with complying.

Chris Blewitt says he was concerned about how the shed appeared to be propped up in his sloping backyard. (Supplied: Chris Blewitt)

Chris Blewitt later learnt that Steve Preston was not a registered builder. (Supplied: Chris Blewitt)

Mr Blewitt said the requests for money happened several times until he had transferred the price of the entire project, after which, he said Mr Preston would then come sporadically.

When weeks dragged into months, Mr Blewitt became concerned and said he wanted $15,000 back so he could hire someone else to finish the project.

Mr Preston argued that meant that Mr Blewitt had effectively terminated the contract.

Eventually he learned Mr Preston had moved to Grafton.

"He wouldn't return my calls, any emails didn't come back, and he'd left town," he said.

Mr Blewitt estimated it cost him up to $15,000 to fix defects and finish off the job before he made a report to NSW Fair Trading about his experience.

In his complaint to Fair Trading, Mr Blewitt said the sheds were incomplete and had defects including damaged Colorbond, inadequate waterproofing and no footings.

"Steve Preston has caused so much damage and can't seem to take any responsibility for it and continues to blame everyone else," Mr Blewitt's statement to NSW Fair Trading said.

"He needs to be stopped so that no one else has to go through the heartache and loss that he has caused."

Chris Blewitt's shed has gaps around the door and walls. (Supplied: Chris Blewitt)

NSW Fair Trading fined Mr Preston $3,000 in 2022 for breach of the Home Building Act, but said no complaints had been lodged against him since.

The NSW Building Commission, which is now the regulator for the state's building industry, said it "strongly" encouraged anyone to make a complaint if they had encountered unlicensed work or contracting, excessive deposit taking or non-compliance with insurance requirements.

"These offences can cause significant detriment to the public and can result in fines, or where repeated offences occur, action on a contractor licence and/or legal proceeding," the spokesperson said.

World.title: The unbreakable trust fuelling cyclists Glasgow medal push
World.content:
In sport, trust between teammates is imperative, but it's hard to imagine a scenario where it's more important than the world of paracycling.

Born with albinism and affected by vision loss associated with the condition, legally blind cyclist Kane Perris rides in tandem with his pilot, Luke Zaccaria.

Now the pair is among the favourites in the men's "tandem b", for vision-impaired cyclists, at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

The trust between them took some time to develop.

"Giving up my control and going against what human nature and the brain says to do, which is … you're riding a bike that I don't have control over steering … on a bunch of wooden planks that are at 44 degrees," Perris said.

Luke Zaccaria and Kane Perris can hit blistering speeds on the track. (ABC News: Ruby Stammers)

"To me, it did take a long time to build that trust in the sport and build that trust in Luke."

The right stuff

Zaccaria discovered Perris on a talent search day, and was immediately struck by his mental strength.

"There were definitely some qualities that really stuck out to me," Zaccaria said.

"We ran the testing, Kane walked in and [impressed with] his attitude and his mindset, which for me is a big thing, it kind of sets people apart.

" But that's something that's not really trainable, that's an inherent quality within him and that really stood out. "

Now they describe their relationship as similar to an old married couple.

Perris and Zaccaria say their relationship resembles that of an "old couple" much of the time. (ABC News: Ruby Stammers)

"We're constantly bickering in the training environment but Luke and I have, like, forged our strength through trust in the relationship we've built over the last six years in riding together," Perris said.

"We have this clear expectation that we're both doing the work.

"Ultimately, it's that trust that makes us go fast."

Speed bumps

Perris is not exaggerating: on a good day, the duo can hit 75 kilometres per hour.

But sometimes the consequences can be disastrous.

It took Perris some time to recover after a harrowing crash at the paracycling world championships in Rio in 2024. (ABC News: Ruby Stammers)

The pair crashed out on the opening day of the paracycling world championships in 2024, and Kane was left with a fractured shoulder, three broken ribs and a punctured lung.

But they licked their wounds and finished fourth in the 1 kilometre time trial at the Paris Paralympics later that year.

Kane says he was at a low ebb mentally when he came to cycling in 2020, in need of a new challenge.

"I really needed something in life that could be the vessel for growth and I never knew that it would be riding bikes in circles at 75km/h but this guy came along and the opportunity came up and I've never looked back.

" What a vessel it's been for my growth as a person, and an athlete. "

Kane Perris and LUke Zaccaria kept the bickering to a minimum during this training session. (ABC News: Ruby Stammers)

Six years after their fateful meeting, Perris and Zaccaria head to the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome in Glasgow to compete in the 1km time trial and sprints, with gold firmly on their mind.

Young star rising

Liliya Tatarinoff has just turned 20, but is already attracting attention for her performances on the track.

She only relocated to Perth a year ago from the New South Wales Central Coast, leaving her family behind to pursue her sporting dreams by training at the WA Institute of Sport under cycling guru Shane Perkins.

"It's been a tough transition, but definitely a worthwhile one," she said.

Liliya Tatarinoff has had her heart set on the Commonwealth Games for years. (ABC News: Ruby Stammers)

"I've had a huge improvement since moving here."

Tatarinoff is a reserve in the team sprint in Glasgow, and will compete in the sprints, keirin and 1 kilometre time trial.

Tatarinoff competed in the world championships last year, her first elite international competition, and said the Commonwealth Games was the "next step".

Tatarinoff is focused on improvement in Glasgow. (ABC News: Ruby Stammers)

"Being selected for the Comm Games is just a huge achievement for me, it's always been a dream of mine ever since I was a little girl," she said.

World.title: Live: Shadow treasurer indicates Coalition support for new WA oil refinery
World.content:
Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie says the Coalition supports a feasibility study into a new oil refinery into a new domestic oil refinery.

The Commonwealth and WA governments will jointly fund a $4 million feasibility study to examine building a new oil refinery in the west.

It's part of a $15 billion package to sure up fuel supplies and expand fuel refining capabilities amid the Middle East conflict which has disrupted global fuel supply chains.

Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, McKenzie says she wants the government to go one step further and scrap the safeguard mechanism.

"We made it very clear in our announcement back in April that we support additional refinery capacity," McKenzie says.

"We want to have fuel security for our nation. That does mean looking at additional refining capacity, but also the things that make refining here in Australia unviable at the moment, which means things like scrapping the safeguard mechanism so that it is financially viable for companies to get on and refine onshore."

So would the Coalition support the development of multiple new oil refineries? McKenzie says she thinks Australia needs more onshore capacity.

World.title: Influencers pushing 'ideal of masculinity' drive male eating disorders
World.content:
Alec White-Cheshire knows too well the damage an eating disorder can do.

First diagnosed at 10 years old, he has been living with anorexia for almost two decades.

It has, he tells the ABC, affected every part of his life: his thoughts, his relationships, even the way he understands the world.

"I have 20 years of living with it," he says.

"I developed as a child with an illness, which has now become entwined into who I am.

"And that's the hardest part to come to terms with.

"You want to feel like this never existed or that you'll never have these thoughts again. But I think the harsh reality is there are certain things you've learned over the years … which will be there forever."

Rather than feeling sadness over his diagnosis, he says, he feels something entirely different.

He feels annoyed.

"When I was 10, [the perception of eating disorders] was quite bad," he says.

"[Now] there are differences. Don't get me wrong, there's a lot of companies and charities and things like that which are doing incredible work.

"But in local communities, it's still very much lacking understanding. Being male, I've experienced dismissiveness.

"People still just don't really understand the impact that any sort of eating disorder has on somebody … it just still seems to be portrayed as more of a choice rather than the illness it is."

Men four times more likely to go undiagnosed with eating disorders

About 365,000 men are living with an eating disorder around Australia, according to the Butterfly Foundation.

On average, just under 2,500 men have been diagnosed each year since 2012.

And men are four times more likely to go undiagnosed for their disordered eating, and less likely to seek help.

Boys aged 16 and under are increasingly reaching out to support services, says Jackson Rose, a counsellor and supervisor for the Butterfly Foundation's helpline.

One of the biggest drivers of disordered eating helpline workers hear about, he says, is pressure from influencers "pushing an ideal around masculinity".

"[It's] very tied into looking a certain way, having that very muscular physique," he says.

"That's also being transferred into a lot of other areas, we're seeing it in television, in movies … that masculinity is presented a certain way."

Stigma remains a frustrating hurdle when it comes to offering real help, Mr Rose adds.

"We see a lot more early intervention around female presentations of eating disorders … but we don't really have as much of that on the male side," he says.

"So when there's a lot more pressure around certain body image types … we're seeing males be a lot more susceptible to that.

"Men make up 33 per cent of the diagnoses of eating disorders.

"But they make up less than 1 per cent of the empirical research [on] eating disorders and eating disorder treatment."

According to the Butterfly Foundation's most recent BodyKind Youth Survey, published last year, 84 per cent of boys aged 12 to 18 reported a desire to be more muscular.

Boys aged 15 to 17 showed the highest prevalence of body dissatisfaction in males, with 48 per cent of those in the 12 to 18 age bracket saying they never or rarely speak positively about their body.

Body image dissatisfaction in men has tripled over the last 25 years, rising from 15 per cent to 45 per cent, according to the Australian Psychological Society.

Former AFL player's off-field battle with bulimia

Former AFL player Brock McLean played 157 games over his 11-year career, during which he became known as a commanding presence on-field with the Melbourne Demons and Carlton Blues.

In private, he was struggling with bulimia nervosa.

"It was back in 2010 when I developed an eating disorder, based on what the coaches were asking me to do," he says.

Brock McLean's professional career spanned more than a decade. (Getty Images: Lucas Dawson)

"I was spending so much time on the sidelines due to an injury, I was desperate to get back and play and I was willing to do anything for it.

"That included compromising my physical health and mental health.

" Eventually, it just took hold of me and I struggled with it for a good five or six years. "

For athletes, the line between healthy and unhealthy behaviours can become blurred, according to eating disorder research institute InsideOut.

A study of Olympic athletes in 2019 found up to 19 per cent of male athletes experienced some kind of disorder.

Sports environments can leave men feeling they have to perform "ideals of masculinity", according to Mr Rose.

"I personally have spoken to some young men who are involved in sports and will often change eating habits," he says.

"[Things like] very strict regimented eating styles, the clean and cut eating and bulking and cutting and cheat meals, all these kind of words people use are often covers for patterns of disordered eating.

"That's often what we see when we look past them."

Loading Instagram content

Now recovered and raising two children with his partner Stephanie, Mr McLean says admitting he needed help changed everything.

"Getting on top of my issues [meant] accepting myself for who I was and finding I could stop blaming myself for things that were outside of my control," he says.

"I was a human being and I was prone to mistakes and I wasn't perfect.

"Men struggle to talk about our emotions. We struggle to talk about our feelings.

"There's still this ingrained toxic culture that talking about our issues or our struggles or our mental health somehow emasculates us.

" But I've learned from experience that in fact, it's the total opposite. It's a huge sign of strength. "

Eating disorder programs 'primarily female'

Eating disorders are one of Australia's deadliest mental illnesses.

As many as a third of those diagnosed will attempt suicide, according a 2023 study published in scientific journal Molecular Psychiatry.

Despite this, a recent Butterfly Foundation Community Insights Report revealed nine in 10 people were not confident spotting the signs of an eating disorder.

More men are getting eating disorders As more men are being diagnosed with eating disorders, experts say stereotypes are still making recovery harder.

"We're already [trying to get] people more aware of male presentations of eating disorders, how to spot those signs in your friends," Mr Rose says.

"But [we need] preventative programs aimed at males, educating parents specifically, because they're probably going to be the first ones who will notice these struggles.

"People don't think about it, but eating disorder programs in Australia are primarily female.

"If you're a male … and you have to go into an inpatient or outpatient program, 90-plus per cent of the people who you will go into that program with will be female.

"So there's no dedicated male eating disorder programs in Australia.

"We really need to … make males feel safe to come forward in the eating disorder space [to] get them back to the lives and the futures they deserve."

Overcoming 'manipulative' mental illness

Alec White-Cheshire now considers himself stable in his recovery, but he knows anorexia is a manipulative disease.

Alec White-Cheshire is in recovery from his eating disorder. (Supplied)

"There's a difference [from] being in a current state of watching everything you do and feeling like, 'Oh my God, is this the illness taking effect?'" he says.

Loading Instagram content

"The illness is very clever in being able to manipulate you into doing certain things and doing new things you may not have before.

"You have to be aware to be able to spot them before they become like a new habit that causes more distress again."

He hopes sharing his story will let other men know they can ask for help, despite the mental and social pressure to hide.

"The hardest part really is that for so long you've been dismissed, and that's really hard to get over," he says.

"Even once you get to the point where maybe someone is willing to listen or give the right support, it's still hard to break that barrier mentally.

"Because you're still not very sure whether that person's genuine.

"[But] you're not alone. No matter how much you feel like that right now, you can get to a point you will feel content and you will actually have your life back.

World.title: Australia won 15 medals in the pool, but this Scottish swimmer with terminal cancer stole the show
World.content:
Glasgow: Australia won an absurd number of medals in the pool on night four of the Commonwealth Games. The Dolphins claimed seven gold, three silver and five bronze to take their overall tally to a somewhat comical 23 victories over England’s four at the Tollcross International Swimming Centre. Lani Pallister, Hannah Casey, Inez Miller and Mollie O’Callaghan after Australia’s 4x200m freestyle victory on Monday in Glasgow. Getty Images But despite another Australian onslaught, the story of the night belonged to a low-profile, 25-year-old Scot who finished equal last in the men’s 100m breaststroke – a race won in thrilling fashion by Sam Williamson. Archie Goodburn has terminal brain cancer. There is a very real chance he will not live beyond the age of 40.



For him to be swimming, let alone standing on the blocks in a major international final listening to the roar of an adoring home crowd, is a testament to his resilience and a fighting attitude that everyone who attended Monday evening’s program could only marvel at. Archie Goodburn of Scotland following his 50m breaststroke final at the Commonwealth Games. PA Images via Getty Images “I’m going to look back on this as an incredible moment in my life,” an emotional Goodburn told a handful of reporters as more prominent medal winners zipped in and out of a busy mixed zone. “I’ve had a lot of tough months over the past few years. Every athlete talks about tough times, but there’s been some really tough times. “This time last year, it was a dark spot.”



Goodburn’s life expectancy was slashed after receiving the news as a 22-year-old in 2024 that he had three “low grade” incurable brain tumours. He had just finished training and was sitting beside Edinburgh’s Commonwealth pool when he received the phone call that changed his life. View post on X Doctors cannot operate because the tumours have spread throughout Goodburn’s brain. He suffered seizures and numbness down the left side of his body. “There is an end point to my life and it’s much earlier than it should be,” Goodburn told the BBC. The prospect of giving up swimming, his one true love, was inconceivable. Remarkably, Goodburn has become faster since his diagnosis, adamant that cancer will not defeat him.



There has also been encouraging news in recent months after Goodburn was granted access to Vorasidenib, a treatment he helped campaign for. The drug has delayed the need for chemotherapy and allowed him to compete in Glasgow. Goodburn arrived hoping to win a medal, but seldom will you find a happier swimmer after finishing equal seventh. The ovation he received from his home crowd was unlike anything else during the night, with Goodburn later describing it as “next level”. But when asked how he manages to remain so positive, knowing his condition could deteriorate at any moment, he paused.



“It’s a really difficult question because this is just a snapshot,” Goodburn said. “This is the highlight of that massive crowd in front of me.” He stopped for 10 seconds, his bottom lip quivering. “Sorry. I want to find an answer for this.” Another five seconds passed. Then came a big breath. “I believe that my own advocacy can make a difference to my own life,” Goodburn said. “The best way I can do that is to be positive about the situation and positive for change.



“I also advocate for the future Archies. I swim for future Archies who want to succeed on an international level. But also young patients and people with brain cancer under the age of 40. Brain cancer is the biggest killer of all cancers for people under the age of 40 in the UK. “Looking back on where I am now … I can’t say a big enough thank you. I’m feeling extremely privileged and very fortunate, very blessed to have even had the chance to take part. “Long may that continue.” Of the nine medal events on the swimming program on Tuesday, Australia won all but two. The Dolphins were always going to dominate the Commonwealth Games, but the regularity of victories has made it difficult for the casual fan to know what’s a good swim and what’s not quite world-class. The biggest surprise came in the women’s 100m freestyle, where a sluggish Mollie O’Callaghan (53.25) settled for silver behind teammate Meg Harris (52.90), who produced arguably Australia’s swim of the night.



Meg Harris, Mollie O’Callaghan and Shayna Jack after Australia went 1-2-3 in the women’s 100m freestyle. Getty Images “It’s my first [win] in the individual 100m freestyle, so I couldn’t be happier with that result,” Harris said. O’Callaghan appears at peace with the fact she is not swimming as well as she would like to due to a back injury. “Meg absolutely killed it tonight,” O’Callaghan said. “I’m just so happy to be here. After my 200 [freestyle], I didn’t feel like myself. You’ve got to adapt at the end of the day. Meg has killed it this year.” Harrison Turner (1:55.38) claimed silver in the 200m butterfly but was left wondering what might have been after fading over the closing stages. Jenna Forrester (4:31.19) was clinical in her 400m individual medley victory but is still a way off Canadian superstar and world record holder Summer McIntosh, while Alex Perkins (56.38) was too strong in the women’s 100m butterfly.

World.title: ‘Gunfight’: At least three shooters at food festival, police say; 15-year-old arrested
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaCrime ‘Gunfight’: At least three shooters at food festival, police say; 15-year-old arrested Gene Johnson Updated July 28, 2026 — 7:35am ,first published 1:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Seattle: Police say there were at least three suspects involved in a food festival shooting near Seattle’s Space Needle over the weekend, and that one of them was among those killed in the violence. In a document filed in juvenile court, where a 15-year-old arrested in the case was making an initial appearance on Monday (Seattle time), police said they believe there were at least three shooters: the 15-year-old; an acquaintance who died at the scene; and “at least one other unknown suspect”. A police officer on patrol after a shooting at Seattle Centre during the Bite of Seattle food festival. AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson “Based on the evidence at the scene, investigators believe” the 15-year-old “and one of the deceased engaged in a gunfight with at least one other unknown suspect”, the document said. The teen was being held in juvenile detention for investigation of firearms violations and first-degree assault ahead of the afternoon court appearance, Mayor Katie Wilson said at a news conference.



Authorities said earlier on Monday they were still looking for an additional suspect, but could not rule out whether that individual was among those killed. “We are trying to identify who that person is,” said Seattle Police Chief Shon Barnes. Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson speaks at a news conference after the shooting. AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson Investigators had said they believed the two suspects were shooting at each other. Police said late Sunday night it was not clear whether any of the victims had been involved in the confrontation between the two shooters. Two people died at the scene, and a third died at a hospital. They were described as two men, ages 19 and 44, and a woman, 56.



The four wounded included a 2-year-old boy, who was in satisfactory condition Monday. The others – two men, ages 23 and 27, and a woman, 39 – were discharged, a hospital spokesperson said. Vendors were allowed to return to the sprawling campus on Monday morning to clean up and collect their equipment and merchandise. World.title: ‘I was running scared’: Australian makes history with brilliant 10,000m gold
World.content:
SportAthleticsCommonwealth Games ‘I was running scared’: Australian makes history with brilliant 10,000m gold Michael Gleeson Updated July 28, 2026 — 7:27am ,first published 11:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Glasgow: Rose Davies looked at the big screen and couldn’t work out how far ahead she was. She had taken the lead with two laps of the 10,000 metres to go, and she was flying. But the screen was deceptive. Were her opponents closing? Had she gone too early? “I was running scared. You know, anything could happen, and I had no idea where the girls were,” she said. Rose Davies celebrates her win and Australia’s first gold at the track. AP “I was trying to look on the big screen, but I was just going as hard as I could in the last 100 metres. But yeah, once I crossed the line, I was very happy.”



Davies became the first Australian to win gold on the Commonwealth Games track on day one of the athletics in Glasgow, the first Australian woman to win a gold medal in this event. She did so beating the two best runners from Africa – the continent that dominates distance running – Kenyan Diana Wanza and Rwanda’s Florence Niyonkuru. The pair just won gold and silver at the African championships in May. With six laps to go, Wanza made a break on a clustered field and opened up a big lead. Davies didn’t completely let her go, but still Wanza had a tough 30-metre gap on her, while Davies’ move to keep Wanza in touch meant she also opened up about a 30-metre gap on Niyonkura at the head of the chasing pack. Davies takes the lead in the 10,000m. AP Davies didn’t panic. She ground at the lead and, sensing Wanza tiring, she pushed with two laps to go and opened up a solid lead of her own. Not that she knew she had. “She did make a pretty hard move with six laps to go, I think, and I knew it was a long way out. So I think I thought if I stayed relatively close I’ll be able to close the gap. And yeah, that’s what I did,” Davies said.



“I could tell she was slowing, but I wasn’t sure how much of a gap I had, and I knew that the race for third, they were coming too, so they could have finished really fast. So I was just still trying to run, you know, my race and run as fast as I could and finish strong. “It was a funny race. It was very up and down, lots of surges. But yeah, I just stayed patient and backed myself in that last 600, and yeah, I’m happy I did.” Davies ran 31:39.32, well ahead of Wanza who hung on for silver in 31:50.13 and Niyonjuru in third in 31:55.47. “It’s huge. Like to beat anyone here is a hard thing, but yeah, I knew they were going to be hard to beat today, and they were probably the main competition. So I just had to stay calm and back myself in,” she said.



“That’s crazy [being the first Australian to win the 10,000m gold]. I’m so happy. I didn’t know that. I just found that out then. So that’s really cool,” she said. A week ago the 26-year-old, who battled injuries early in her career, broke the national 5000m record when she came third in the London Diamond League. That day too she had to run down a leader, but unlike in Glasgow, in London she unwisely didn’t keep pushing but sat on the lead and was herself swamped at the line. She learnt from that. Davies celebrates claiming gold in the women’s 10,000m. Getty Images “Instead of going past her [in London] I sat and I got kicked on in the last bit. So tonight I just tried to stay calm and when I saw she was slowing, I felt really strong. So I just thought, back myself in and go as hard as I could. And yeah, I’m stoked I did that. “I feel like you have to back yourself in, no matter how fast other girls are. And I’ve been training really well, racing really well, so there was no reason why I couldn’t beat them. I just kept reminding myself that.”



Man on a mission: Rohan Browning finished second in his 100m heat on Monday. Getty Images Browning slams 100m qualifying rules Earlier on the first day of athletics competition, sprint champion Rohan Browning slammed the 100m qualifying at the Games as “plainly unfair” and manufactured to get certain runners into the finals. Runners with the eight fastest times in the first half of this calendar year have automatically been placed in the semi-finals without having to run heats. Only the 17 fastest times in the heats will advance to the semi-finals in Glasgow. Ordinarily, the first two finishers in each heat, and then two or three of the next fastest runners across all heats, would advance.



“It’s an unheard-of progression. It’s extremely weird,” said Browning, an Olympic and world championships semi-finalist. Related Article Live

Commonwealth Games Commonwealth Games 2026 LIVE: Gold rush in Glasgow: Swimmers rake in medals as Aussie grabs first athletics gold with brilliant run “I mean, it’s gusty out there. So when they just make up these rules about eight guys get to go through and the rest of the field goes through like on the time trial rather than, you know, first or second across the line, the reality is some heats will get better conditions than others. So I don’t know what’s going on. “I think when you turn up to a championships, you’re prepared to run three rounds, and the reality is you’ve got to run hard for all of them. So, you know, I felt like I was running hard out there, even if it also felt a little awkward.” Browning qualified for the semi-finals, placing second in his heat with a time of 10.24s.



“Of course, it’s not fair. Clearly, it’s not fair,” Browning said of the fact eight athletes had automatically advanced to the semi-finals without running a heat. “Like it’s clearly been engineered to try to achieve a desired outcome. Whatever’s motivated that decision, I don’t know what it is or if it’s reasonable or not. But clearly, it’s not fair. I think everyone would agree on that. “You would expect to [advance after automatically finishing second] but it’s possible that people might get a slow heat and nobody might go through from that heat. “Look, at the end of the day, this sport is meritocracy at its finest. If you’re quick enough, you go through.



“So I suppose you could say those guys have earned their place through the season. In all likelihood, they’re probably the guys who are going to make the final, regardless. But you just don’t know … some guys might be injured, some guys might be out of shape.” Further to Browning’s point, for the final heat of the morning, there was a big +3.9m/s tailwind which would make any time illegal, as far as records go. But there was no adjustment for the wind in any of the heats. While all heats had some form of tailwind, most were only light, although that changed late. World.content:
Cheek Media founder Hannah Ferguson has announced she will run against Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in the seat of Grayndler at the next election.

The podcaster and commentator said Australians were fed up with the major parties and felt they weren’t being listened to.

Hannah Ferguson said she was born in Marrickville in Sydney’s Inner West and lives in the Grayndler electorate. Oscar Colman

“He’s been the member for 30 years, and I feel like, as a young person in Australia, that I do not feel represented at a local level by him. I think this is an incredibly progressive electorate that demands and deserves more than a politician who is beholden to the interests of the gambling lobby and the fossil fuel industry,” Ferguson told Sunrise.

“More people need to be standing up, putting their head above the parapet, and challenging people like the prime minister,” she said.

Ferguson said she planned to step away from the company she founded, Cheek Media, next year to campaign full-time.

The 28-year-old had previously indicated she would run as an independent candidate for the Senate, but said community members had urged her to take on Albanese in the lower house.

The Victorian government may avoid a bruising leadership challenge, with Jacinta Allan understood to be reconsidering her position within hours of an expected caucus vote.

World.title: Australia won 15 medals in the pool, but this Scottish swimmer with terminal cancer stole the show
World.content:
Glasgow: Australia won an absurd number of medals in the pool on night four of the Commonwealth Games. The Dolphins claimed seven gold, three silver and five bronze to take their overall tally to a somewhat comical 23 victories over England’s four at the Tollcross International Swimming Centre. Lani Pallister, Hannah Casey, Inez Miller and Mollie O’Callaghan after Australia’s 4x200m freestyle victory on Monday in Glasgow. Getty Images But despite another Australian onslaught, the story of the night belonged to a low-profile, 25-year-old Scot who finished equal last in the men’s 100m breaststroke – a race won in thrilling fashion by Sam Williamson. Archie Goodburn has terminal brain cancer. There is a very real chance he will not live beyond the age of 40.



For him to be swimming, let alone standing on the blocks in a major international final listening to the roar of an adoring home crowd, is a testament to his resilience and a fighting attitude that everyone who attended Monday evening’s program could only marvel at. Archie Goodburn of Scotland following his 50m breaststroke final at the Commonwealth Games. PA Images via Getty Images “I’m going to look back on this as an incredible moment in my life,” an emotional Goodburn told a handful of reporters as more prominent medal winners zipped in and out of a busy mixed zone. “I’ve had a lot of tough months over the past few years. Every athlete talks about tough times, but there’s been some really tough times. “This time last year, it was a dark spot.”



Goodburn’s life expectancy was slashed after receiving the news as a 22-year-old in 2024 that he had three “low grade” incurable brain tumours. He had just finished training and was sitting beside Edinburgh’s Commonwealth pool when he received the phone call that changed his life. View post on X Doctors cannot operate because the tumours have spread throughout Goodburn’s brain. He suffered seizures and numbness down the left side of his body. “There is an end point to my life and it’s much earlier than it should be,” Goodburn told the BBC. The prospect of giving up swimming, his one true love, was inconceivable. Remarkably, Goodburn has become faster since his diagnosis, adamant that cancer will not defeat him.



There has also been encouraging news in recent months after Goodburn was granted access to Vorasidenib, a treatment he helped campaign for. The drug has delayed the need for chemotherapy and allowed him to compete in Glasgow. Goodburn arrived hoping to win a medal, but seldom will you find a happier swimmer after finishing equal seventh. The ovation he received from his home crowd was unlike anything else during the night, with Goodburn later describing it as “next level”. But when asked how he manages to remain so positive, knowing his condition could deteriorate at any moment, he paused.



“It’s a really difficult question because this is just a snapshot,” Goodburn said. “This is the highlight of that massive crowd in front of me.” He stopped for 10 seconds, his bottom lip quivering. “Sorry. I want to find an answer for this.” Another five seconds passed. Then came a big breath. “I believe that my own advocacy can make a difference to my own life,” Goodburn said. “The best way I can do that is to be positive about the situation and positive for change.



“I also advocate for the future Archies. I swim for future Archies who want to succeed on an international level. But also young patients and people with brain cancer under the age of 40. Brain cancer is the biggest killer of all cancers for people under the age of 40 in the UK. “Looking back on where I am now … I can’t say a big enough thank you. I’m feeling extremely privileged and very fortunate, very blessed to have even had the chance to take part. “Long may that continue.” Of the nine medal events on the swimming program on Tuesday, Australia won all but two. The Dolphins were always going to dominate the Commonwealth Games, but the regularity of victories has made it difficult for the casual fan to know what’s a good swim and what’s not quite world-class. The biggest surprise came in the women’s 100m freestyle, where a sluggish Mollie O’Callaghan (53.25) settled for silver behind teammate Meg Harris (52.90), who produced arguably Australia’s swim of the night.



Meg Harris, Mollie O’Callaghan and Shayna Jack after Australia went 1-2-3 in the women’s 100m freestyle. Getty Images “It’s my first [win] in the individual 100m freestyle, so I couldn’t be happier with that result,” Harris said. O’Callaghan appears at peace with the fact she is not swimming as well as she would like to due to a back injury. “Meg absolutely killed it tonight,” O’Callaghan said. “I’m just so happy to be here. After my 200 [freestyle], I didn’t feel like myself. You’ve got to adapt at the end of the day. Meg has killed it this year.” Harrison Turner (1:55.38) claimed silver in the 200m butterfly but was left wondering what might have been after fading over the closing stages. Jenna Forrester (4:31.19) was clinical in her 400m individual medley victory but is still a way off Canadian superstar and world record holder Summer McIntosh, while Alex Perkins (56.38) was too strong in the women’s 100m butterfly.

But you just don’t know … some guys might be injured, some guys might be out of shape.” Further to Browning’s point, for the final heat of the morning, there was a big +3.9m/s tailwind which would make any time illegal, as far as records go. But there was no adjustment for the wind in any of the heats. While all heats had some form of tailwind, most were only light, although that changed late. Cheek Media founder Hannah Ferguson has announced she will run against Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in the seat of Grayndler at the next election.

The podcaster and commentator said Australians were fed up with the major parties and felt they weren’t being listened to.

Hannah Ferguson said she was born in Marrickville in Sydney’s Inner West and lives in the Grayndler electorate. Oscar Colman

“He’s been the member for 30 years, and I feel like, as a young person in Australia, that I do not feel represented at a local level by him. World.title: Man arrested in Russia over accusations of spying for New Zealand
World.content:
A man has been arrested in Russia on accusations of spying for New Zealand.

In a statement, the Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) said the Russian Federation had "identified and stopped the illegal activity of a citizen of the Russian Federation suspected of committing treason".

The FSB said it had established a Khabarovsk resident, born in 1971, "proactively established" contact with the New Zealand Security Intelligence Service.

New Zealand's intelligence services are part of the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance which includes Australia, Canada, Britain and the United States.

The FSB said the contact was done for "for selfish motives, on instructions from a foreign intelligence service, using foreign email services and instant messengers, transmitted information to the foreign intelligence service that could be used against the security of the Russian Federation".

The FSB said it had opened a criminal case against the man and he was being investigated under Article 275 (treason) of the Russian Criminal Code.

The man has been remanded in custody.

"The Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) once again draws the attention of citizens to the fact that treason is punishable by criminal penalties under Russian law, including life imprisonment."

The Moscow Times reported the man was arrested in the south-east city of Khabarovsk.

Video footage by FSB shown by Russian media showed authorities rushing over to the man on a street pavement and pinning him to the ground before locking him in handcuffs.

The video showed the man being taken into custody and his home searched.

The information hasn't been independently verified.

Both Foreign Minister Winston Peters and the minister with responsibility for the spy agencies Chris Penk referred comment to the NZSIS.

A spokesperson for the NZSIS told RNZ it had a longstanding practice of not commenting on what "may or may not be operational matters".

"It should also be noted that Russian state media are often not the most reliable source of accurate reporting," the spokesperson said.

The New Zealand government has placed sanctions against those supporting Russia's war against Ukraine.

Earlier this year, Peters annouced more sanctions against cyber actors and online platforms supporting Russia's war on Ukraine.

More than 2000 groups, individuals and vessels had been sanctioned since the war began.

Peters has consistently said New Zealand will hold Russia and its enablers accountable.

World.title: Children missing school because parents can't afford fuel, social worker says
World.content:
Rising fuel costs hit rural school attendance Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Social workers are warning some children in rural areas are missing out on too many days at school because their parents cannot afford the fuel to drive them each day.

It comes as the number of people on the Jobseeker benefit continues to rise and thousands more receive hardship grants for food.

The government is also seeking advice on whether to keep the support for families affected by the fuel crisis.

As a school social worker, Eloise Jowitt saw first hand the pressure on families who could not afford fuel to drop their children at school.

She said this was a big problem for students who lived in South Auckland's rural outskirts, whose closest school was not within walking distance.

"I'll pick them up because, I mean, that's if you want a kid to come to school, sometimes that's the easiest solution," Jowitt said.

"Kids want to come to school. These kids, they're always happy. I have kids that are ready, waiting for me, excited to come to school."

Eloise Jowitt, a school social worker. RNZ / Amy Williams

She works at Manurewa Central School and said on a rainy day, there were noticably fewer pupils because many lacked raincoats or even shoes.

"It's falling upon us more than ever before to support these families in need. I'm seeing the cost of energy, the cost of fuel and the cost of food are harder than it's ever been for families to afford."

She said it was common to see whole families sleeping in one room using body heat to stay warm.

"I know for one mum, she's got a heat pump in the house, but it's never on. Her form of heating is when she uses the dryer in the evening, and that's how she's currently heating her house."

Jowitt is among Presbyterian Support Northern's team of school social workers who are linked to about 96 primary and intermediate schools in the upper North Island.

Its chief executive Shaun Greaves said referrals have increased and it was hearing this winter was harder for families struggling to pay for food, heating and fuel.

Presbyterian Support Northern chief executive Shaun Greaves. Supplied / Presbyterian Support Northern

"One of the major things we're seeing is the cost of fuel and the impact it has at some of our rural schools. In some cases kids aren't able to get to school because of the cost," he said.

"That typicllally is keeping the child at home because that's the cheapest option, not that they want to keep them at home, that's what they can afford to do."

Presbyterian Support Northern is among charities with winter appeals to help those most in need.

"If we can support those children today, we can really shape their future for years to come. Any support the government can give around the cost of fuel, food, electricity, any of things to ease the burden absolutely goes a long way."

The Ministry of Social Development's latest figures show in the June quarter there were 218,500 people on the Jobseeker benefit - up nearly 2500 from the same period last year.

In that time, 86,500 people got off the benefit and into work - up nearly 6000.

And thousands more received special needs grants for food - up just over 8000.

Even so, Eloise Jowitt often accompanied parents to appointments with Work and Income and was seeing more grants being declined.

"This is their last option, and they're being told that they should be managing their budget better when I've seen week to week how they struggle," she said.

"Even as a social worker advocating for their needs, it's still hard to get those grants across the line and I'm seeing a lot more declines. It is really hard to see."

Manurewa Central School principal Mike Piper said the cost of living was the greatest barrier to regular school attendance.

"You want to see them come to school and when you get that attendance and you know that you can give them a little bit of a hand, whether it's feeding them, the odd bit of stationary every now and then, it's awesome that way," Piper said.

"We just want them at school and we do our best to make sure they get here, take away the barriers and get them here."

World.title: Vaccination a great early Christmas present, expert says
World.content:
Dr Mamaeroa David on protecting against winter illness Morning Report Download MP3 5m

A senior doctor is urging people to get vaccinated, even if it means paying for it, as winter illnesses spread.

Data shows rhinovirus is dominating illnesses picked up in primary care, while hospitalisations are being driven by RSV, influenza and Covid-19.

Dr Mamaeroa David, a senior Maori medical advisor with the Immunisation Advisory Centre and an Auckland GP, told Morning Report on Tuesday her three kids were "getting hit with a whole lot of snot germs" before the school holidays.

"We're very glad to have that little reprieve over the school holidays. But the cold has set in good and proper now and it's escalating all the respiratory diseases this winter.

"I just had a look at the PHF Science website last night, and the rhinovirus was chugging along nicely even before the school holidays…

"So we've got cold and flu viruses, adeno, rhino, those are the like, snotty but happy children. But RSV and flu viruses, our kiddies get a little bit more sicker with that, and adults as well. Adults do get sick from those, and RSV is definitely starting to increase."

While rhinovirus dominated positive tests, hospitalisations were led far and away by RSV.

New Zealand has one of the world's highest rates of serious illness caused by RSV, and experts have been calling for a national childhood prevention programme to be set up.

A recent trial in Australia of administering vaccinations to women of childbearing age and giving newborns doses of Beyfortus, a long-acting monoclonal antibody injection (a short-lasting form of passive immunisation), nearly halved hospitalisations from the virus ahead of the winter peak. Beyfortus does not teach the immune system how to recognise the virus like a vaccine would, according to the US Centers for Disease Control.

In New Zealand, a vaccine is available for older people - Arexvy - but it is not funded, and can cost several hundred dollars.

Even vaccines that are available and cheap - such as that for this year's influenza - are not being taken up numbers health officials would like.

"We're still lagging in our flu vaccination rates," David said. "I'm telling everybody, you know, I think the flu hasn't kicked in. I think this current burst of respiratory diseases is RSV-related mostly.

"That is not a funded vaccine for the elderly. You can pay for it. So anyone who's having a birthday or early Christmas present… tell your kids to pay for your Arexvy vaccine.

"Flu is funded for over 65 and for people with other comorbidities. So definitely go and see if you're funded for flu.

"If you're not funded for flu vaccine, only $24 from most outlets - Chemist Warehouse, et cetera. So it's a bit of advertising for our vaccine providers, but you know, I don't think the flu's hit yet, but it is coming. So you've still got time to get your immunisation."

If you do get sick, David said there are new rapid antigen tests (RATs or RAT tests) which can tell you which illness it is.

"We used to do it just for Covid, but you do have multi-RATs now that test for influenza A and B and RSV, respiratory syncytial virus… and Covid of course, there's the four on there. That can be really useful to let you know what you have and so you're not getting antibiotics for a virus.

World.title: Digital connectivity 'no longer a luxury' - TUANZ
World.content:
The Technology Users Association (TUANZ) says the government needs to take the lead to address gaps in New Zealand's digital infrastructure and policy direction.

TUANZ's latest report indicates 87 percent of New Zealanders had access to ultra-fast fibre broadband, but access wasn't shared equally, with one in 10 households having no internet access at home, and Māori, Pasifika, disabled people and low-income households disproportionately affected.

"Rural communities also continue to face higher costs and more limited connectivity options than their urban counterparts," TUANZ chief executive Craig Young said.

The organisation's sixth and final paper on digital policy, released over the past six weeks, focuses on access and inclusion.

"Digital connectivity is no longer a luxury. It underpins education, healthcare, employment, business, emergency response and participation in modern society. If we want a more productive, resilient and inclusive New Zealand, we need to treat connectivity as essential infrastructure," Young said

"Over the last two decades, New Zealand has made significant progress in building world-class digital infrastructure. The opportunity now is to ensure no community is left behind."

TUANZ set out four key areas for action on connectivity:

Recognise connectivity as core infrastructure

Establish a National Connectivity and Resilience Register

Co-design affordable connectivity solutions

Mandate inclusive design for digital public services

Young said TUANZ was keen to see recommendations set out in its policy papers used to inform a national digital strategy, which he said was currently missing from the government's portfolio of policies.

"There was work on one before this current government came in, and then those were quietly shelved," he said.

"That was one of their pillars in the Go for Growth document, but we've seen very little come out that on how they'll actually make that happen."

Young said the lack of digital leadership was a common thread in its six policy papers.

"We really do not have an overarching direction on anything digital, whether it's connectivity, data transparency, whether it is AI.

World.title: TikTok-related spending worth $1.2 billion to NZ annual economy - report
World.content:
TikTok-related spending contributed an estimated $1.2 billion to the country's GDP last year and supported nearly 10,000 jobs, according to a new report from economic consultancy Infometrics.

But not everyone is convinced.

The report, commissioned by TikTok, was based on surveys of 1000 adult weekly users and 700 business decision-makers, carried out by consumer research firm Nielsen.

It found about 309,000 New Zealand businesses were using TikTok at least monthly to promote themselves, while 671,000 users reported spending money each month after seeing products, services or places on the platform.

Infometrics chief executive and principal economist Brad Olsen said the scale of business use was notable, particularly because firms did not necessarily need large followings or expensive production to reach customers.

Brad Olsen. LDR

"The opportunity here is that as a business you can put something up and once it goes viral, once you manage to get that connection going, it spreads," Olsen said.

He said that reach was translating into reported business outcomes, with surveyed firms reporting a median sales uplift of between 20 and 30 percent from their TikTok activity.

The report put the average self-reported sales uplift at about 24 percent.

The report said TikTok-related off-platform spending was worth an estimated $1.2b in GDP, while business promotional activity on the platform contributed a separate estimated $515m in GDP.

Infometrics said the two figures should not be added together because some spending by users would overlap with the sales gains reported by businesses.

The report also found younger businesses were more likely to use the platform, with 63 percent of firms less than five years old saying they used TikTok monthly, compared with 21 percent of businesses operating for more than 16 years.

Infometrics said the results were based on survey responses and economic modelling, including self-reported spending and sales uplift figures, rather than direct measurement of transactions.

But Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said the report needed to be taken "with a sack of salt" because it was assuming that the activity would not have happened elsewhere if TikTok was not present in New Zealand.

It had also not tackled the tax questions around multinationals making money in this country,

World.title: Commonwealth Games: Swimmer Lewis Clareburt stuns Glasgow rivals - and himself
World.content:
Kiwi swim sensation Lewis Clareburt has stunned everyone - including himself - with a stunning gold-medal performance over 200m butterfly at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.

Clareburt stormed home over the final 50 metres of the race to overhaul Aussies Harrison Turner and Matthew Temple to retain the crown he won four years ago at Birmingham.

Commentators were speechless to describe his swim. At halfway, Clareburt was seventh, 1.58 seconds behind Turner, who had qualified fastest from the morning's heats.

He closed to fourth with 50 metres remaining and was the only swimmer to crack 30 seconds over the final length of the pool to pip his rival at the touch.

"I thought I was out of that race the whole time," Clareburt told RNZ afterwards.

"I came to the second-to-last lap and was still feeling amazing, so I was, like, 'I better start swimming faster'.

"I knew from four years ago the last 50 is anyone's race, so had the energy at the right time and to turn around and see the number one next to your name on the board is a pretty special feeling."

He immediately celebrated his win by smashing the water in his lane and could not stop smiling throughout the medal presentation.

Clareburt said, physically, he felt great afterwards.

"I felt like I could run through a brick wall. I didn't expect to win that race.

"I thought it was going to be a lot harder than previously and the talent in the field showed that."

World.title: As it happened: Glasgow Commonwealth Games, day four
World.content:
Swimmer Lewis Clareburt has won New Zealand's first gold medal at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, successfully defending his 200m butterfly title.

The Australian-based Kiwi sat midfield for the majority of the race, but powered home over the final 50 minutes to snatch victory from Australian Harrison Turner. Australian Matthew Temple was third.

"I thought I was out of that race the whole time," Clareburt told RNZ afterwards.

"I came to the second-to-last lap and was still feeling amazing, so I was like, 'I better start swimming faster.'

"I knew from four years ago the last 50m is anyone's race, so had the energy at the right time, and to turn around and see the number one next to your name on the board is a pretty special feeling."

Clareburt said physically he felt great afterwards.

"I felt like I could run through a brick wall. I didn't expect to win that race - I thought it was going to be a lot harder than previously, and the talent in the field showed that."

It took New Zealand's medal haul to eight - one gold, four silvers and three bronze, all in the pool.

Clareburt won silver in the 200m individual medley earlier in the programme.

He will also attempt to defend his 400m medley title on Wednesday.

Joshua WILLMER takes Silver for New Zealand in the 100m breaststroke S89. . 2026 Glasgow Commonwealth Games at Tollcross International swimming Centre Glasgow. Photosport

'Silver is better than bronze'

Para swimmer Josh Willmer took the silver medal in the men's 100m breaststroke SB9 final.

Willmer touched third, but was promoted to second after Fernando Lu of Canada was disqualified. Willmer's time of 1m 11.44s was also a games record for his classification.

Beau Matthews of Australia won the gold.

Willmer was shocked when he found out his medal had been upgraded.

"Unreal, yeah, I had no idea," Willmer told RNZ. "Bummer for the guy that got [disqualified] but what an upgrade - silver is better than bronze."

New Zealand also collected bronze in the women's 4x 200 freestyle relay, with the team of Erika Fairweather, Caitlin Deans, Eve Thomas and Milana Tapper finishing behind Australia and England.

Hazel Ouwehand finished eighth in the women's 100m butterfly final.

Carter Swift finished fifth in his semi-final of the men's 100m freestyle to sneak into the final eighth-fastest. Australian Kyle Chalmers was the top qualifier, with a time almost a second faster than Swift.

Savanah-Eve Martin and Amber George qualified sixth- and seventh-fastest for the final of the women's 50m backstroke, with Canadian Kylie Masse quickest.

World.title: Opportunity Party still open to working with National despite Christopher Luxon ruling it out
World.content:
Political update: Luxon rules out working with Opportunity Morning Report Download MP3 7m

The Opportunity Party leader says their door is always open, despite National ruling out including them in a potential coalition.

During Monday's post-cabinet media conference, National leader Christopher Luxon said he would not do business with any party that wanted to raise taxes.

His office later confirmed he had ruled out working with Opportunity.

The fledgling party is on the cusp of entering Parliament according to the latest RNZ-Reid Research poll, which put it at 4.7 percent - just shy of the 5 percent threshold.

Opportunity's leader Qiulae Wong has consistently said it would work with any party, and she told RNZ that position had not changed following Luxon's comments.

"We are still here, ready and willing to have that conversation when he is," she said.

"I think there's a lot on our policy platform, what we stand for, that National would want to further, and I think we'd be a good constructive partner for them."

That was still possible, she said.

"They might need us to form a government, in which case I guess their tune might change."

Opportunity's flagship policies include establishing a universal basic income of up to $370 a week, and a 1.75 percent annual tax on the value of urban land and 0.5 percent on rural land.

Wong said her party's policy would cut taxes for 70 percent of New Zealanders, raise them slightly for about 10 percent, and leave 20 percent about the same.

She had not had any formal conversations with Labour or National about working together following the election, she said.

Wong urged the major parties to move on from "tribal politics", saying New Zealanders had told her they were sick of it.

"The more that we try to put New Zealand voters into a box of either left versus right, means that we rule out the idea of people kind of working constructively together on some of our really big gnarly issues, like climate change, and AI, and how we're going to grow the economy.

"That old school way of doing politics really needs to end, we've got to do things differently."

Labour's campaign chair Kieran McAnulty said the party would set out who it could work with "very shortly".

Labour leader Chris Hipkins. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Party leader Chris Hipkins subsequently told Morning Report his announcement on which parties Labour would work with before Parliament rises on 1 October, and that would include detailing bottom lines for negotiations to form a government, as well as areas of alignment with other parties.

"We're going to do that based on principle, rather than who we've got the pip with on any given day," he said.

"We're seeing other parties releasing their election policies, and we're releasing our own election policies and I'm going to make these decisions and the Labour Party's going to make these decisions based on principle of where there's alignment."

Labour had "absolutely ruled out" supporting a land tax or a wealth tax, he said.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins speaks to Corin Dann Morning Report Download MP3 9m

"Unlike Christopher Luxon I'm not a pushover, I'm not going to turn around after the election and say 'all the things I said I wouldn't do before the election, I'm going to change that through coalition negotiations. I've been very clear, I'm ruling that out, it's not going to happen."

ACT leader David Seymour said he was surprised to hear Luxon rule out working with Opportunity - because he thought he had already done so.

World.title: Cabo Verde stunner gets people's vote as best World Cup goal
World.content:
Cape Verde has made more World Cup history with Sidny Lopes Cabral winning the public vote for goal of the tournament.

Lopes Cabral's curling shot into the far top corner of the Argentina net was a stand-out moment at the World Cup where the unheralded African team made a stellar debut.

His goal tied defending champion Argentina at 2-2 in extra time of their thrilling Round of 32 game in Miami Gardens. Cape Verde would eventually lose 3-2.

Lopes Cabral's goal was voted best of the 308 goals scored at the tournament, ahead of Eldor Shomurodov's delicate lob for Uzbekistan against DR Congo and Wilson Isidor of Haiti scoring with a powerful rising shot against Morocco.

FIFA drew up a shortlist of 12 goals for public voting that closed Monday.

Sidny Lopes Cabral headed for the stands to celebrate with fans and family after scoring a screamer for Cabo Verde against Argentina. (Getty Images: ISI Photos/Eston Parker)

Lopes Cabral's celebration also entered World Cup lore as he broke free of teammates reaching to grab him before climbing into the tribune to hug his girlfriend and look for his mother.

"Before the game, I'd told my mom and my girlfriend that if I scored, I'd run over to them," he said.

"When I got there, I saw my mom crying. She hadn't even realised I was right there. Everyone was busy tending to her because she had fainted when I scored."

Cape Verde defied both World Cup finalists in its four games, after goalkeeper Vozinha's stand-out display saw his team open with a 0-0 draw to stun eventual champion Spain.

AP

World.title: Aussie Rohan Browning clips 'unfair' 100m surprise sprung on sprinters
World.content:
Just a day or two before the start of the athletics program at the Commonwealth Games, the public was made aware that the top eight 100 metre sprinters in the rankings would be given a free ticket into the semifinals in a break from tradition.

It left the rest of the field, including Australians Rohan Browning and Eddie Nketia, to duke it out in a mass time trial across 11 heats.

It was a significant change to the usual system where everybody runs the heats and the top two in each race are automatic qualifiers, with the remaining runners trying to get through on times.

Both Australians finished second in their heats, but Browning could not enjoy the moment after going through in 10.24 seconds in heat seven with four more to come.

Browning said the new rules were as much of a surprise to him as they were for the rest of us.

Glasgow 2026 day four live Australia wins nine gold medals across the pool, athletics track and in the gymnastics on day four in Glasgow.

"It's an unheard of progression, it's extremely weird. It's really hard to know, I have no idea what times have been run, I have no idea where I sit in the placings," he said, asking reporters to clue him in on where he sat in the standings.

"It's gusty out there, so when they just make up these rules about eight guys get to go through and the rest of us goes through on a time trial rather than first or second across the line, the reality is some heats will have better conditions than others, so I don't know what's going on."

Browning made the cut in 16th as the second slowest qualifier and compatriot Eddie Nketia was fourth fastest overall with his 10.07

Browning, who was a controversial inclusion in the team ahead of Josh Azzopardi, said he always turns up prepared to run three rounds but the other folks, including countryman Lachie Kennedy, do not have to.

Eddie Nketia looked powerful as he finished second in his heat. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

"It's not fair, clearly it's not fair," he said.

"It's clearly been engineered to try to achieve a desired outcome. Whatever's motivated that decision, I don't know what it is or if it's reasonable or not, but clearly it's not fair. I think everyone would agree on that."

Nketia said it was out of his control so he was not going to worry too much about it, and Browning acknowledged the best response is probably to just run fast.

Aussie sprinter feels 'robbed' Josh Azzopardi opens up after missing out on selection as a 100 metres runner in Australia's athletics team for the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.

"At the end of the day this sport is meritocracy at its finest; if you're quick enough you go through, so I suppose you could say those guys have earned their place," he said.

"In all likelihood they were probably the guys paying the best odds to make the final regardless, but you just don't know. Some guys might be injured, some guys might be out of shape. I don't even know when they took the performances from."

National record holder Torrie Lewis is experiencing both sides of the coin in the women's events, running the heats in the 100m but granted the automatic progression in the 200m.

"Having a day off in the middle is perfect, so I'm really happy with that," he said after winning her heat in 11.15 seconds to finish as the second-fastest qualifier.

"It would've been better if it was first [past the post], just to eliminate the wind because it's so gusty going around, but what can you do? Just be the fastest no matter what."
